lines.text: 1.1 GENERAL
Belize, formerly British Honduras, is part of the
Yucatán Peninsula which projects northward from
the Central American mainland and separates
the Gulf of Mexico from the Caribbean Sea. This
peninsula extends almost to western Cuba, an island
with which it has much in common physiographi-
cally, geologically and botanically. Lying between
bounded, in the north and part of the west by Mexico,
and in the remainder of the west and the south by
Guatemala. The country is 278 km long, with a
maximum mainland width of 109 km. In addition to
the mainland area of 22,157 km?, numerous coral
inlets, or 'cayes', totalling 543 km' are to be found
between 3 and 80 km offshore along almost the
country's entire length.
The low coastal plain is mainly covered by man-
grove swamp, from which the land rises gradually
toward the interior. The Belize River divides the
country into two approximately equal-sized regions.
To the north are considerable areas of low tableland,
sloping gently eastwards from a western elevation
which rarely attains a height of more than 130 m. The
two principle rivers draining this area, Rio Hondo
and New River, run northward to Chetumal Bay.
From the 16-24 km wide coastal plain in the south,
the land rises to form the Cockscomb and Maya
Mountains, while further inland is the Mountain Pine
Ridge which is 300-1,020 m above sea level. These
areas are drained by numerous streams and rivers.
Victoria Peak, in the Cockscomb Mountains, is the
highest point in Belize at 1,120 m.
Although the population has increased from
120,000 in 1970 to approximately 240,000 in 1993,
the density is still relatively low at under 11/km?.
Almost one-third of this population lives in the old
capital, Belize City, with the other six major towns,
Belmopan, Corozal Town, Dangriga, Orange Walk
Town, Punta Gorda and San Ignacio, accounting for
the remaining fifty percent of the urban population.

Introduction
Rainfall, along with topography, geology and soil
variation, plays a large part in influencing the varia-
tions seen in the forest and other flora. Although
Belize lies wholly within the tropics, the climate is
sub-tropical, tempered for nine months of the year by
trade-winds along the humid coastal plain. Coastal
temperatures range from 15-38°C, with a mean shade
temperature of 27°C; inland the range is greater.
Annual rainfall varies, but ranges from a mean of
1,300 mm in the north (Corozal District) to 4,250 mm
in the extreme south (Toledo District). These figures
are recorded from low altitude weather stations; a
rapid rise of precipitation occurs with increasing
elevation. Rainfall is thus highest in the south and in
the central mountain mass, and decreases rapidly
toward the north. A dry season usually extends from
February to May, with a shorter dry period in Au-
gust.
Since 1931, six hurricanes have struck Belize. The
most serious, Hattie, devastated the country in 1961,
causing severe destruction and loss of life. As a result
of advanced early warning systems, Greta caused
minimal loss of life in 1978, but the authors wit-
nessed the devastation of forest growth and resultant
loss of epiphytic orchid habitat. Several years later,
dislodged orchids, particularly Encyclia and Maxilla-
ria species, Mormolyca ringens (Lindl.) Schltr. and
Trigonidium egertonianum Batem. were to be seen
still surviving on the forest floor.

The central and southern coastal plain soils are
similar to those of the northern plain, but are mainly
covered by sandy detritus which supports only pine
forest and dry savannah. The riverine alluvial belts
support a rich rain forest, characterised by the pres-
ence of cohune palm. These soils, derived from the
igneous rocks of the central mass, are deeper and
more fertile than those of the northern plain, although
more acidic. The valleys and lower hill slopes of the
central mountain region contain a deep red fertile soil
in granitic areas; this soil becomes shallower in slate,
schist and quartzite areas.
The southern Toledo region has deep fertile soils in
the well-drained areas, but much of the land consists
of heavy water-logged clays.
The Mayan Indians are known to have cultivated
large areas of Belize between 300 B.C. and 900 A.D.,
growing such crops as maize, beans, cassava and
coco. Terraces remaining from this civilisation are
still visible on limestone hills in the Chiquibul area of
Cayo District. Present-day Mayan farmers still oper-
ate the milpa system of their ancestors, whereby
annual slashing and burning of new tracts of forest is
undertaken. This shifting agriculture has been res-
ponsible for the clearance of forest from large tracts
of land.
Early British settlers and African slaves realised
the potential of logwood (Haematoxylon campechia-
nuт L.) for dyes and mahogany for timber, and by
1850, Belize City had developed as a trading port.
Mexican Cedar (Cedrela mexicana M.J. Roem) and
rosewood (Dalbergia stevensonii Standley) were the
other important timbers found in the hinterland.
The establishment of British Honduras as a crown
colony in 1862 saw the development of large agricul-
tural estates, with cane being planted in Toledo and
the northern districts for sugar and rum production.
With the riverine system being the virtual sole means
of transport, poor communications into the interior
did much to lessen the economic prosperity. In the
late 1890's, cattle production increased in Cayo and
the northern districts following the importation of
Guinea grass (Panicum maxiтum Nees) and Pará
grass (Panicum purpurescens Opiz). By 1900
Creole-populated riverside and Carib-populated
coastal smallholdings were established, growing
corn, bananas and plantains. Coconuts have always
been important, particularly in the first quarter of this
century. In 1937, sigatoka leaf spot and Panama dis-
ease of bananas caused a decline in that industry,
forcing farmers to expand citrus, especially orange
and grapefruit, production in the Stann Creek Valley.
Introduction
Small areas of rice production have been developed
in Belize and Toledo Districts.
Clearance of land in the northern districts for the
production of sugar and cattle has resulted in a se-
rious loss of orchid habitat, particularly in Corozal.
Likewise, removal of logwood and other timbers has
taken its toll of epiphytic orchid habitat in logwood
stands and rain forest. Citrus plantations, which are
particularly resistant to permanent damage by hurri-
canes, have, however, produced a micro-environ-
ment suitable for many epiphytic species. Indeed
some species, such as Psygmorchis pusilla (L.) Dod-
son & Dressler, are rarely found outside of grapefruit
groves. Catling, Brownell & Lefkovitch (1986) and
Catling & Catling (1987) have carried out some
interesting ecological studies of epiphytic orchids in
a Belizean grapefruit orchard.
Over the last 15 years, Belize has witnessed a
relatively large influx of refugees from the civil war
in El Salvador. The majority of these were milpa
farmers, with a resultant ribbon development along-
side roads and rivers, particularly in Cayo and Stann
Creek Districts. This practice has led to further orchid
habitat loss.
The Government of Belize, in efforts to safeguard
the environment, has ensured the protection of over
30 reserves and parks, ranging from as little as 8
hectares, to over 107,000 hectares in the case of the
Chiquibul National Park. When declared as a pro-
tected area under the National Park System Act of
1981, activities such as felling, burning, injuring or
removing any trees, squatting, grazing or pasturing of
cattle, hunting, shooting and fishing are prohibited
In other areas, licences and permits are issued
under Belize's Forest Act for controlling forestry, to
ensure sustained utilisation by monitoring of the re-
sources.
This bodes well for the future of the native orchid
species in Belize, and the People and Government
must be congratulated for their attempts to link con-
servation with development.

plants found in Belize are widely distributed along
the Atlantic slope from Mexico to northern South
America. However, a considerable number are
known on the Central American mainland only from

lines.text: the Yucatán Peninsula, as well as being found in
Cuba, Jamaica and other West Indian islands. Some
may even be found in southern Florida. The locally
common pine in Belize, Pinus caribaea Morelet,
although reaching as far south as Nicaragua, is found
primarily in Florida and the West Indies. Of particu-
lar interest is the occurrence of South American
species, mainly from Brazil and the Guianas, which
are found on the Central American mainland only in
Belize: two orchids foundby
examples; Koellensteinia tricolor (Lindl.) Rchb. f.
and Maxillaria discolor (Lodd. ex Lindl.) Rchb. f.
The terrestrial orchid, Eulophia alta (L.) Fawc. &
Rendle, on the other hand, has a very wide distribu-
tion, being found in Florida, Mexico, the West Indies,
Central America, northern South America and even
tropical Africa. Despite its botanical connections
with other areas, the Yucatán Peninsula does, how-
ever, have many endemic species such as the log-
wood tree and many sapodillas (Sapotaceae).
Standley and Record (1936) produced an excellent
catalogue and description of the forests and other
vegetation types of Belize, and much of the informa-
tion and classification given here is based on their
book.
The mainland forests may be conveniently divided
into mangrove (3%), savannah and pine (18%) and
rain (79%), with various subdivisions.
The dominant species in the mangrove forests is
the red mangrove (Rhizophora mangle L.) which
occurs along the coast and in tidal swamps and la-
goons.
Of the savannahs, the brackish water type replaces
mangrove above the tidal limits and has a tall sedge
growth on a dark-coloured silt. Neither the mangrove
forest nor this savannah type supports orchids. The
fresh water savannahs occur along coastal streams
and on the sites of inland lagoons. A similar sedge
growth is dominant and is subject to seasonal flood-
ing and fire damage. Inland savannahs developed
upon a shallow sandy soil overlying marl in the north,
alluvial clay or grits in the central area and northern
Toledo coastal plain, and the parent rock of the moun-
tain mass. In the moister areas, shallow sands subject
to water logging support a sedge growth. while the

may be found in the fresh water and inland savan-

and fresh water savannahs. The delta and flats above
high tide and the river levees in the coastal plain
contain white and black mangroves (Laguncularia
racemosa (L.) Gaertn. f. and Avicennia nitida Jacq.)

(Chrysobalanus icaco L.), provision tree (Pachira
aquatica Aubl.) and swamp kaway (Pterocarpus
officinalis Jacq.) to form the tidal levee forest. The
confra palm (Manicaria saccifera Gaertn.) is predo-

The brackish savannah contains palmetto palm and

waika chewstick (Symphonia globulifera L.) in the
central and southern regions. Santa María (Calophyl-

savannahs and is home for several orchid species,
particularly of the genus Encyclia.

fed by subsurface drainage of the watershed, are to be
found criss-crossing the area.

Pine Ridge because of its rich orchid flora. Scattered

boo and various oaks, all of which are fire resistant.

the Yucatán Peninsula, as well as being found in

although reaching as far south as Nicaragua, is found

and Maxillaria discolor (Lodd. ex Lindl.) Rchb. f.
The terrestrial orchid, Eulophia alta (L.) Fawc. &
Rendle, on the other hand, has a very wide distribu-
tion, being found in Florida, Mexico, the West Indies,
Central America, northern South America and even
tropical Africa. Despite its botanical connections
with other areas, the Yucatán Peninsula does, how-
ever, have many endemic species such as the log-
wood tree and many sapodillas (Sapotaceae).
Standley and Record (1936) produced an excellent
catalogue and description of the forests and other
vegetation types of Belize, and much of the informa-
tion and classification given here is based on their
book.
The mainland forests may be conveniently divided
into mangrove (3%), savannah and pine (18%) and
rain (79%), with various subdivisions.
The dominant species in the mangrove forests is
the red mangrove (Rhizophora mangle L.) which
occurs along the coast and in tidal swamps and la-
goons.

and on the sites of inland lagoons. A similar sedge
growth is dominant and is subject to seasonal flood-
ing and fire damage. Inland savannahs developed
upon a shallow sandy soil overlying marl in the north,
alluvial clay or grits in the central area and northern
Toledo coastal plain, and the parent rock of the moun-
tain mass. In the moister areas, shallow sands subject
to water logging support a sedge growth. while the
deep, better drained sands display a predominance of
true grasses.

lines.text: population, commonly shade the ravine heads and
form a marginal forest along streams, where the soil
is somewhat richer. Shrubs are rare in the open pine-
land, but the orchids Cattleya bowringiana O'Brien,
with its attractive purple flowers, and Encyclia beli-
zensis (Rchb. f.) Schltr. ssp. belizensis are locally
common on rocky outcrops, whereas Sobralia mac-
rantha Lindl., with its short-lasting flowers, is seen
growing in clumps among the grasses, sedges and
legumes of the herbaceous ground cover.
The vegetation along the streams and upland
marshes consists of small shrubs and trees, alternated
with marsh and rocky areas. Steep grassy banks and
dense palmetto palms add to the variety. Of the trees,
Clusia spp. dominate, with scattered pines and Billy
Webb (Sweetia panamensis Benth.), along with
pockets of the teabox shrub (Myrica cerifera L.). The
vegetation bordering these streams undoubtedly
offers the richest variety of Belizean epiphytic
orchids, particularly Maxillaria species. The larger
streams along the western edge of the Mountain Pine
Ridge are liable to become torrents after heavy rains,
but they equally rapidly subside. Here the vegetation
is similar, but is interspersed with areas of tall rain
forest growing on the rich black alluvia of the flood
plain. Clumps of the tree fern (Sphaeropteris myosu-
roides (Liebm.) Tryon) occur in densely shaded val-
leys. Cattleya bowringiana and Encyclia belizensis
subsp. belizensis are again locally common, with the
rarer Encyclia alata (Batem.) Schltr., growing along
river banks, particularly of the Rio On. A belt of
marginal forest consisting of scattered pines, oaks
and silver pimentos with an undercover of shrubs and
herbs exists between the pines and the rain forest on
open rocky banks of the larger streams. The forest of
the limestone borderland contains pines and oaks, but
the undergrowth gives way to lime-loving species
such as the abundant bayleaf palm (Sabal mayarum
H.H. Bartlett).
The forest of the bordering limestone hills contains
many species typical of the dry deciduous forest of
the northern part of the Yucatán Peninsula, such as
manzanilla (Coccoloba cozumelensis Hemsl.) and
redwood (Erythroxylon areolatum L.). Many of the
species are found in the wooded swamps of southern
Campeche in Mexico, and the adjoining Department
of Petén, Guatemala, and are significant in interpreta-
tion of the vegetation of the peninsula. These species
are among those dominating the cactus thicket and
deciduous forest of Yucatán and Quintana Roo, Me-
xico. Their presence as relics on dry hills in the much
higher rainfall southern areas of Belize may indicate
that the climate was considerably drier or that Mayan
clearances favoured growth of these plants. This
Introduction
vegetation on the tops of the limestone hills suggests
that cactus thicket and deciduous forests were more
extensive than now. Coelia bella (Lem.) Rchb. f. and
several species of Epidendrum are among the many
orchids which may be found in these areas.
The intermediate rain forest occupies the niche
between swamp or pine forest and advanced rain
forest. Common tree species include mahogany, al-
though much has now been removed, Santa María,
Billy Webb, negrito (Simarouba amara Aubl.), cher-
ry (Pseudolmedia spuria Griseb.) and madre de
cacao (Gliricidia sepium (Jacq.) Kunth. ex Walp.).
Three associations of this so-called 'broken ridge' are
apparent. In the north, swamp and pine forests give
way to bayleaf palm, give-and-take palm (Cryoso-
phila argentea H.H. Bartlett), sapodilla and silly
young (Pouteria amygdalina (Standley) Baehni); the
dry pine forest of the central region is colonised by
whitemalady (Aspidospermastegomeris (R.E.
Woodson) R.E. Woodson), pigeon plum (Licania
hypoleuca Benth.), carbón (Hedwigia panamensis
Engl.), introduced mountain cabbage palm (Euterpe
oleracea Engel) and tree fern, whereas in the central
and Toledo regions,swamp and savannah forests
give way to nargusta (Terminalia amazonia (J.F
Gmel.) Exell), Santa María, waika chewstick and
yemeri (Vochysia hondurensis Sprague).
Mountain rain forest on ridges of high elevation in
the central region is an intermediate between the
mountain pine and advanced forest of the lower
slopes. Since these mountains are remains of meta-
morphic rocks intruded into the older limestones
which are now almost eroded, it is remarkable that
this region has similar species to the savannahs i.e.
waika chewstick, Santa María, swamp fig and Pur-
diaea belizensis, as well as mountain cabbage palm
and species of oak.
Advanced rain forest is characterised by the
cohune palm, which often forms a dense sub-canopy,
and undergrowth which ousts dicotyledonous spe-
cies. Several species of tall trees are found, along
with abundant shrubs which are replaced in the den-
ser forest by palms or small ferns. Epiphytes abound,
particularly orchids, bromeliads, aroids, ferns and
mosses. Tree species include the tall spreading
cotton-tree (Ceiba pentandra (L.) Gaertn.), Santa
María, nargusta, yemeri, mamee apple (Pouteria
mammosa (L.) Cronquist), prickly yellow (Zanthoxy-
lum kellermanii P. Wilson), hog plum (Spondias
mombin L.), rubber (Castilla elastica Cerv.) and figs.
Cedar and breadnut (Brosimum alicastrum Sw.) are
found only on calcareous soils.
The Maya cultivated large areas of rain forest,
leaving the cohune palm for shade and oil. This

lines.text: TRIBE TROPIDEAE DRESSLER
1. Corymborkis Thou.
Terrestrial plants with short, sympodial, creeping
rhizomes; roots fasciculate, wiry. Stems erect, terete,
unbranched, leafy, bamboo-like. Leaves plicate, dis-
tichous or spirally arranged, sessile. Inflorescences
axillary, paniculate, few-to many-flowered. Flowers
distichously arranged, often not opening widely,
white, pale green or yellow, fragrant; pedicel short,
twisted. Sepals and petals subsimilar, narrow, basally
connivent. Lip spathulate, with 2 longitudinal keels
embracing the column below. Column elongate, slen-
der; rostellum erect, bifid; pollinia 2.
A pantropical genus of about five species. One is
known from Belize.
EtymoLoGY. From the Greek corymbos (a cor-
ymb) and orchis (orchid), referring to the inflores-
cence of the type species, C. corymbis Thou.
Corymborkis forcipigera (Rchb. f.) LO.Williams.
in Bot. Mus. Leafl. Harvard Univ. 12: 237 (1946).
Type: Granada, Warscewicz (holo. W!).
Macrostylis forcipigera Rchb. f. in Bonplandia 2: 96
Corymborchis cubensis Acuña in Bol. Téc. 60, Est.
Exp. Agron. Santiago de Las Vagas: 51 (1939).
Plant terrestrial, tall, stout, erect, up to 2 m tall. Stem
terete. Leaves large, crowded on the upper part of
stem, elliptic-lanceolate, distichous, sessile, many-
nerved, up to 45 cm long and 7.5 cm wide. Inflores-
cences 1 to 3, lax, corymbose, paniculate, axillary, up
to 12 cm long. Flowers greenish-white, arcuate;
floral bracts lanceolate, acute, clasping the base.
Sepals canaliculate, fleshy; dorsal sepal linear, in-
curved, up to 19 mm long and 2.5 mm wide; lateral
sepals linear-oblanceolate, acute, up to 15 mm long
and 2.5 mm wide. Petals oblanceolate, thinner than
Species descriptions

sepals, up to 13 mm long and 3.5 mm wide. Lip
arcuate-decurved, spatulate, canaliculate below with
2 longitudinal keels within, up to 14 mm long. Col-
umn arching, apex bluntly acute, reflexed, up to 12
mm long.
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. The West Indies, Me-
xico, Belize, Guatemala and Costa Rica.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Toledo District. Rare.
HABITAT. In rich soil and humus, in forest and
thickets.
FLOWERING SEASON. July.
ETymoLoGY. From the Latin forcipis (a pair of
tongs, a forceps) and gero (to bear) in allusion to the
flower shape.
NoTE. Reported by Catling & Catling (1988) but
not seen by us. Previous reports by Standley & Rec-
ord (1936), Williams (1956) and Spellman (1975)
described Corymborchis flava (Sw.) O. Kuntze as
occuring in Belize. These reports were based on
herbarium specimens at AMES (M. E. Peck 610) and
are referrable to C. forcipigera. The difference be-
tween these two species has been reviewed by Correll
SUBTRIBE GOODYERINAE KLOTZSCH
Plants terrestrial or semi-epiphytic, small, arising
from a creeping rhizome. Stems erect, sheathed by
bracts or the bases of petiolate leaves. Leaves cauline,
with distinct petioles which are expanded into an
infundibuliform sheath. Inflorescence a terminal ra-
ceme of small flowers. Dorsal sepal and petals arch-
ing over the lip; lateral sepals free. Lip 3-lobed, with
the base dilated into a prominent sack-like spur. Col-
umn short; rostellum erect, bipartite, clearly defined
with tapering segments after the viscidium has been
removed.

Plant terrestrial, erect, slender, up to 30 cm tall. Scape
leafy, pubescent above. Leaves shortly petiolate,
ovate-lanceolate, acute, dark to pale green flecked
with white, abaxially purple to light green, up to 9 cm
long and 3.3 cm wide. Inflorescence racemose,
loosely-flowered; bracts linear-lanceolate, scarious.
Flowers white or greenish-white. Sepals somewhat
pubescent; dorsal sepal linear, up to 5 mm long and
1.8 mm wide; lateral sepals lanceolate, up to 5.5 mm
long and 1.8 mm wide. Petals linear-oblanceolate, up
to 5 mm long and 1.5 mm wide. Lip up to 8.5 mm
long including saccate spur, lateral lobes recurved
and minutely ciliate. (Fig. 1).

and Costa Rica.

Small to medium-sized terrestrial plants with a creep-

secondary stems. Leaves basal, clustered in lower
part of stem, fleshy, several, petiolate from inflated

lines.text: GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Belize and Costa Rica.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Exact locality not
known. Rare.
HABITAT. In elfin forests.
FLOWERING SEASON. October.
ETymoLoGY. From the Latin erosus (having an
irregularly toothed margin).
NoTE. Reported by Siegerist (1984) but not seen
by us.
Terrestrial or semi-epiphytic herbs, relatively small,
arising from a creeping rhizome. Stems erect, sheath-
ed by bracts or the bases of petiolate leaves. Leaves
with short petioles that surround the base of the stem,
usually reticulate-veined. Inflorescence a terminal
raceme. Flowers very small, fleshy. Dorsal sepal and
petals arch over the lip; lateral sepals are free. Lip
3-lobed, with the base dilated into a prominent sack-
like spur; rostellum entire, flat, elliptic to suborbicu-
lar, sometimes emarginate.
There are more than 100 species distributed in the
American tropics and subtropics. Two are known
from Belize.
L.A. Garay (1977) transferred some species of
Erythrodes to the new genus Platythelys on the basis
that Erythrodes,astypifiedbythe type species E
latifolia Blume, has an erect, bipartite, clearly
defined rostellum with tapering segments after the
viscidium has been removed while the rostellum of
Platythelys is different. It is entire, flat, elliptic to
suborbicular, its tip is commonly ruptured by the
removal of the viscidium, rarely, it appears to be
emarginate. Moreover, the tiny flowers are very
fleshy.
ETYMoLoGY: From the Greek platys (flat) and
thelys (pertaining to a woman) in reference to the
broad flat rostellum.
Leaves ovate-lanceolate; inflorescence sessile, usual-
ly densely flowered....
Leaves lanceolate-linear; inflorescence subsessile,
often loosely flowered...

and 2 cm wide; leaf-sheaths and petiole translucent.

acute, up to 7 mm long. Flowers white, not fragrant,

Photo. 9,10).

Plant terrestrial, slender, up to 30 cm tall. Roots short,

or less elliptic, with a satin-like appearance, up to 6
cm long and 2.7 cm wide; petiole short. Inflorescence
spicate, densely many-flowered; peduncle up to 21
cm long; sheaths pale green. Flowers minute, white,
sometimes tinged with pink; pedicellate ovaries up to
5 mm long. Sepals and petals recurved; sepals ovate,
obtuse, up to 2 mm long and about 1.2 mm wide;
petals linear to narrowly ovate, up to 1.5 mm long and
0.5 mm wide. Lip erect, subcircular, deeply concave-
saccate, apiculate, with 2 lateral auricles at the base,
up to 1.5 mm long and 2 mm wide when spread.

Plants terrestrial with slightly hairy roots. Leaves
basal, several and petiolate. Scape slender, erect and
bracteolate. Inflorescences terminal, densely many-
flowered, spicate. Flowers very small. Sepals free,
occasionally connate; lateral sepals with a subdecur-
rent base. Petals parallel. Lip unguiculate, claw ad-
nate to the base of the lateral sepals. Column short
with an inflated clinandrium.
Seven species are native to the American tropics
and subtropics. One is known from Belize.
EtymoLogY. From the Greek belos (a dart) and
glossa (a tongue) in reference to the shape of the lip
of the type species, Spiranthes costaricensis (Rchb.

Beloglottis costaricensis (Rchb.f.) Schltr. in Beih.
Bot. Centralbl. 37 (2): 364 (1920). Type: Costa Rica,
Öersted (holo. W!).
Spiranthes costaricensis Rchb.f. in Bonplandia 3:
S. bicaudata Ames, Orchid., 7: 126 (1922).
Plant terrestrial, slender, up to 40 cm tall. Scape
almost concealed by tubular-acuminate bracts. Lea-
ves basal, elliptic-oblong, acute, tapering at base, up
to 19 cm long and 6 cm wide; petioles narrow.
Inflorescence spicate, racemose or compact. Flowers
green or white, tubular, flaring at apex, strongly fra-
grant of violets. Sepals slightly hairy on outer sur-
face, up to 7 mm long and 1.5 mm wide; lateral sepals
united for a short distance at base forming a sack,
linear-lanceolate; dorsal sepal linear, concave at base.
Petals linear, recurved at apex. Lip with a broad claw,
triangular-ovate, apex ciliate, up to 6 mm long. Col-
umn short, up to 3 mm long, bristly on anterior
surface. (Fig. 4).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. The West Indies, Me-
xico and Central America.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Toledo District.
HABITAT. In moist mixed forest, on slopes or
along roadsides.
FLOWERING SEASON. February and March.
EtymoLogY. From Costa Rica, and the Latin ad-
jectival suffix -ensis, referring to the country of origin
of the type specimen.
Small to medium-sized terrestrial or epiphytic herbs
with fleshy, fasciculate roots. Leaves basal, in
rosettes, petiolate, lacking prominent venation. Sca-
pe slender, several-sheathed. Inflorescence spicate,
laxly to many-flowered. Flowers small, membrana-
ceous, pubescent on outer surface. Sepals similar,
basally connate forming a cylindrical tube, free
above with spreading segments. Petals connivent
with dorsal sepal. Lip broadly auriculate, the claw
free from the sepaline tube. Column free, elongate;
rostellum acute, bifid; pollinia 2, deeply-divided, cla-
vate.
There are about 70 species recorded from Florida,
the West Indies, Central and South America. Four are
known from Belize.
EtyMoLogY. From the Greek kyklos (a circle) and
pogon (a tail of fire with divided ends, bearded) in
reference to the sepals (reddish in dry condition)
which emerge from the circular sepaline tube.

lines.text: 1. Cyclopogon comosus (Rchb.f.) Burns-Bal. &
Greenwood in Orquídea (Méx.), 10 (1): 92 (1986).
Type: Mexico, Leibold (holo. W!).
Spiranthes comosa Rchb. f. in Linnaea 18: 408
Beadlea comosa (Rchb.f.) Hamer & Garay, Orquid.
El Salvador 3: 48 (1981).
Plant terrestrial. Leaves basal, dark green and silvery-
striped, up to 5 cm long and 1.7 cm wide; petiole up to
2 cm long. Scape erect, up to 17 cm long.
Inflorescence spicate, 5-to 10-flowered; floral bracts
attenuate, up to 10 mm long. Flowers small; ovary
echinate. Sepals up to 7 mm long, olive-brown;
lateral sepals connate at base. Petals translucent with
a green nerve, up to 5 mm long. Lip up to 8 mm long,
apical portion white, dilated into a reniform lobe with
thickened margins, basal portion olive-green with
two conspicuous whitish translucent calli. Column
bifid at the apex, short, up to 2 mm long.
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Mexico, Belize and El
Salvador.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Exact locality not
known. Rare.
HABITAT. In cloud forest.
FLOWERING SEASON. March.
EtymoLogY. From the Latin comosus (bearing a
tuft of hairs or leaves).
NoTE. Reported by Catling & Catling (1988)
based on a specimen by Schipp S-833 (AMES).
2. Cyclopogon cranichoides (Griseb.) Schltr. in
Beih. Bot. Centralbl. 37 (2): 387 (1920). Type: Cuba,
C. Wright 3293 (holo. GH; iso. K!).
Pelexia cranichoides Griseb., Cat. Pl. Cub.: 269
Sauroglossum cranichoides Ames. in Proc.
Spiranthes cranichoides (Griseb.) Cogn. in Urb.,
Symb. Antill. 6 : 338 (1909).
Beadlea cranichoides (Griseb.) Small, Fl. Southeast
Plant terrestrial, slender, up to 28 cm tall. Leaves few,
broadly ovate in a rosette, petiolate; blade up to 6 cm
long and 2.5 cm wide; petiole channelled, up to 4 cm
long. Inflorescence many-flowered; peduncle pale
brownish-purple, pubescent above, up to 20 cm long,
with several white-spotted sheaths. Flowers rather
small and inconspicuous. Sepals pale green, up to 6
mm long and 1.5 mm wide; dorsal sepal suffused
with purple; lateral sepals spreading. Petals spa-
tulate, spreading at the tip, white edged with green or
7 Cyclopogon
Biol.
purple veins, up to 4.5 mm long. Lip white, 3-lobed,
curved, widest near the middle, up to 5.5 mm long;
lateral lobes broad, erect, clasping and adherent to the
column. Column white, up to 4 mm long. (Fig. 5;
Photo. 14).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Florida, Cuba, the West
Indies, Belize, Guatemala and Venezuela.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Toledo District. Rare.
HABITAT. In dense wet forest.
FLOWERING SEASON. January and February.
EtymoLogY. From Cranichis (another orchid
genus) and the Greek adjectival suffix -oides (indicat-
ing a resemblance to) referring to the similarity of the
two plants.
3. Cyclopogon elatus (Sw.) Schltr. in Fedde, Repert.
Sp. Nov., Beih. 6: 53 (1919). Type: Jamaica, Swartz
s.n. (holo. BM!).
Satyrium elatum Sw., Prodr.: 119 (1788).
Neottia minor Jacq., Ic. Pl. Rar. 3: t.601 (1793).
Spiranthes elata (Sw.) L. C. Rich. in Mém. Mus. Par.
Beadlea elata (Sw.) Small ex Britton in Brooklyn
Bot. Gard. Mem. 1: 38 (1918).
Sarcoglottis elata (Sw.) P.N.Don in Hort. Cantabr.
Plant terrestrial, up to 25 cm tall. Leaves few, up to 4,
petiolate; blade dark green, variegated with pale
silvery-green, up to 15 cm long and 3.2 cm wide;
petiole grooved, up to 7 cm long. Inflorescence pube-
scent above; peduncle pinkish-brown, up to 13 cm
long, with several sheaths. Flowers numerous, nodd-
ing. Sepals dark green to pinkish, up to 2 mm wide at
base; dorsal sepal concave above the middle, rec-
urved at the tip, up to 7 mm long; lateral sepals
somewhat upcurved, up to 9 mm long. Petals slender,
brownish below, white above with a brown mid-vein,
upcurved at the tip, up to 6 mm long. Lip constricted
above the middle, with two incurved projections at
the base and a prominent terminal lobe, up to 8.5 mm
long; terminal lobe white; lower portion green,
becoming white at base, with erect margins clasping
the column. Column up to 3 mm long. (Photo. 15).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Florida, the West Indies,
Mexico to South America.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Toledo District. Rare.
HABITAT. In dense wet forest.
FLOWERING SEASON. March and April. Flowers
last about two weeks.
EtymoLogY. From the Latin elatus (tall) referring
to the size of theplant.

small and inconspicuous. Sepals pale green, up to 6
mm long and 1.5 mm wide; dorsal sepal suffused
with purple; lateral sepals spreading. Petals spa-
tulate, spreading at the tip, white edged with green or

Plant terrestrial, up to 25 cm tall. Leaves few, up to 4,
petiolate; blade dark green, variegated with pale
silvery-green, up to 15 cm long and 3.2 cm wide;
petiole grooved, up to 7 cm long. Inflorescence pube-
scent above; peduncle pinkish-brown, up to 13 cm
long, with several sheaths. Flowers numerous, nodd-
ing. Sepals dark green to pinkish, up to 2 mm wide at
base; dorsal sepal concave above the middle, rec-
urved at the tip, up to 7 mm long; lateral sepals
somewhat upcurved, up to 9 mm long. Petals slender,
brownish below, white above with a brown mid-vein,
upcurved at the tip, up to 6 mm long. Lip constricted
above the middle, with two incurved projections at
the base and a prominent terminal lobe, up to 8.5 mm
long; terminal lobe white; lower portion green,
becoming white at base, with erect margins clasping
the column. Column up to 3 mm long. (Photo. 15).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Florida, the West Indies,
Mexico to South America.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Toledo District. Rare.
HABITAT. In dense wet forest.
FLOWERING SEASON. March and April. Flowers
last about two weeks.
EtymoLogY. From the Latin elatus (tall) referring
to the size of theplant.

lines.text: 4. Cyclopogon prasophyllum (Rchb. f.) Schltr. in
Beih. Bot. Centralb. 37 (2): 393 (1920). Type: Guate-

Spiranthes prasophylla Rchb. f., Beitr. Orch.
Beadlea prasophyllum (Rchb. f.) Hamer & Garay,
Orquid. El Salvador, 3: 27 (1981).
Plant usually epiphytic, small, up to 16 cm tall when
in flower but often less. Leaves 3 to 5 in a basal
rosette, arising from a few fleshy swollen roots, lan-
ceolate, dark green, glossy, becoming pinkish-red
with prominent green veins when old, up to 7 cm long
and 2 cm wide, with a short petiole. Inflorescence
spicate, many-flowered, solitary, somewhat longer
than the leaves, slightly pubescent. Flowers greenish
or purplish-green with a white lip, subtended by a
large lanceolate bract, not fragrant, up to 1.4 cm long
including the pedicellate ovary. Dorsal sepal lanceo-
late, up to 6 mm long and 2 mm wide; lateral sepals
similar but up to 8 mm long and 2mm wide. Petals
linear, up to 5 mm long and 1 mm wide. Lip cons-
tricted above the middle, up to 6.5 mm long. Column
up to 4 mm long. (Photo. 16).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Belize to Panama.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Cayo and Toledo Dis-
tricts. Rare.
HABITAT. Epiphytic or terrestrial in dense moist
forest.
FLOWERING SEASON. January and February.
ETYMOLOGY. From the Greek prasos (leek-green)
and phyllon (a leaf) referring to the colour of the
leaves.
Plants small to miniature, facultative epiphytes. Lea-
ves basal, rosulate with ciliate blades. Scape short,
erect. Inflorescences terminal, a densely compact,
capitate spike. Flowers very small, hidden by cilio-
late bracts. Sepals basally connate forming a tube;
dorsal sepal with a decurrent base, partially adnate to
the column; lateral sepals connate at base forming a
sac. Petals decurrent at base. Lip canaliculate, paral-
lel with column, broadly unguiculate. Column
slender with a long decurrent incurved foot.
A genus of about 13 species native to the American
tropics and subtropics. One is known from Belize.
ETYMOLOGY. From the Greek eurys (broad) and
stylis (a pillar or column) describing the shape of the
column which, in the original material unfortunately
was deformed.
8. Eurystyles Wawra
8 Eurystyles
Eurystyles borealis A. H.Heller in Fieldiana, Bot.
31: 279 (1968). Type: Nicaragua, Heller 10861
(holo. F).
Plant epiphytic, small, up to 3 cm tall. Stems absent or
reduced; roots white, fleshy. Leaves basal, up to 6 in a
rosette, elliptic, vernicose when living, margins un-
dulate, glossy, up to 27 mm long and 16 mm wide.
Inflorescence terminal, pendent; peduncle slender,
white-ciliate, head of flowers up to 1.5 cm long.
Flowers up to 25, often fewer, white tinged with
green, not fragrant, sessile, up to 6 mm long, not
opening widely; bracts pubescent, up to 1 cm long.
Sepals with echinate pubescence, up to 3.5 mm long
and 1 mm wide. Petals free, up to 3.5 mm long and 1
mm wide. Lip spathulate, 3-lobed at apex. Column up
to 4.5 mm long. (Fig. 6; Photo. 17).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Central America.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Toledo District. Rare.
HABITAT. On trees, especially vertical trunks, in
dense wet forest.
FLOWERING SEASON. December and January.
Flowers last about ten days.
ETymoLoGY. From the Latin borealis (northern).
Plants terrestrial, small, commonly aphyllous during
anthesis. Roots fleshy, pubescent. Stems slender,
erect. Leaves small when present. Inflorescences ter-
minal, a spirally twisted spike. Flowers small. Sepals
subsimilar, divergent; dorsal sepal ovate-lanceolate,
concave; lateral sepals spreading. Petals variable. Lip
menbranaceous, panduriform with a short claw. Col-
umn short, dilated above, basally produced in a short
foot.
A genus of three species native to Mexico, Belize,
Trinidad, Venezuela, Bolivia and Brazil. One is
known from Belize.
ETYMOLoGY. From the Greek lyra (a lyre) and
glossa (a tongue) describing the shape of the lip
characteristic for all species.

Plant terrestrial, short, stout with thick roots. Leaves
2 or more, basal. Stem puberulent, slender, up to 25
cm long. Leaves elliptic-oblanceolate, glabrous, thin,
petiolate, up to 12 cm long and 5 cm wide. Inflores-
cence a loosely flowered spike of 10-20 flowers,
subtended by lanceolate bracts. Flowers small, white
tinged with green-yellow, cystoliths present. Dorsal
sepal lanceolate, up to 4 mm long and 1.5 mm wide.
Lateral sepals linear- oblong, acute, up to 6 mm long.
Petals adnate to dorsal sepal, oblanceolate, up to 4
mm long and 1.2 mm wide. Lip oblanceolate, up to
5.5 mm long and 1.2 mm wide. Column up to 2 mm
long. (Fig. 8; Photo. 19).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Belize and Guatemala.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Toledo District.
HABITAT. Remnant rainforest in soil over lime-
stone rock.
FLOWERING SEASON. Not known.
ETymoLoGY. From Petén in Guatemala and the
Latin suffix -ensis (indicating the country or place of
growth or origin) indicating the area the plant was
originally found.
NOTE. Mesadenella tonduzii (Schltr.) Pabst &
Garay was reported as occuring in Belize from a
collection south of Belmopan as Spiranthes tonduzii
(Adams & Cribb 1985). This specimen (Adams 227
K!) has been reexamined (Catling & Catling 1988)
and is referable to M. petenensis rather than M. tondu-
zii.

roots. Leaves in basal rosette, petiolate. Inflores-

sized. Dorsal sepal erect, forming a hood with the

A genus of about 50 species widely distributed in

Plant a cluster of thick, fleshy, whitish roots, super-

Panama and western South America.

lines.text: Plant terrestrial, a small and very delicate herb con-
sisting of 2 to 5 leaves arising from a cluster of very
thick, fleshy roots. Leaves up to 15 cm long, basal,
petiolate; leaf-blade oval, dark green with prominent
silvery veins, up to 7 cm long and 4 cm wide.
Inflorescence from the centre of the leaves, un-
branched peduncle which is dark greenish-red, en-
closed in a number of sheaths, up to 30 cm tall.
Flowers numerous and small, subglobose, up to 7
mm long including the ovary, dark greenish with a red
lip, not opening widely, not fragrant. Sepals similar,
free to base. Petals with inner margins agglutinate to
dorsal sepal. Lip cordate-cochleate,rather fleshy.
Column very short, arcuate, basally forming an in-
curved foot. (Fig. 10; Photo. 22).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Cuba, the West Indies,
Mexico, Belize and Guatemala.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Belize District. Rare.
HABITAT. In forest on limestone hills, often in
pockets of moist humus on the ground, between tree
roots or on old stumps.
FLOWERING SEASON. January and February. Flow-
ers last several weeks.
EtymoLogY. Named after Charles Wright (1811-
1885), an American botanist and the collector of the
type specimen.
Plants terrestrial. Roots fasciculate, tuberous. Leaves
often absent when flowering spike produced, basal or
cauline, sessile. Stem erect, vaginate or bracteolate.
Inflorescences terminal, a subdense, many-flowered
raceme. Flowers large, often showy. Sepals free,
subsimilar, connivent; dorsal sepal concave; lateral
sepals decurrent on the column-foot forming a spur-
like extension. Petals joined to to dorsal sepal. Lip
sessile, arcuate. Column short, stout, basally ex-
tended in a long foot.
A genus of about 10 species native to the American
tropics and subtropics. One is known from Belize.
EtymoLoGY. From the Greek sakkos (a sack or
bag) and koilos (hollow) describing the spur-like
extension formed by the bases of the lateral sepals.

Plant terrestrial, a cluster of thickened, fleshy, tube-
rous roots. Leaves appear after the inflorescence has
faded, deciduous, usually up to 6-leaved in a rosette,
lanceolate, glossy, up to 20 cm long and 2.5 cm wide.
Inflorescence up to 50 cm tall, upright, flowers borne
on the upper third of a shortish brown peduncle with
white pubescence, with about 7 sheathing bracts
which are usually reddish in colour. Flowers numer-
ous, densely clustered, only opening slightly, up to 3
cm long with the ovary, not fragrant, white pube-
scent; ovary dark greenish-brown marked with three
paler lines leading to the base of each sepal, well
developed at flowering time. Sepals vary in colour
from greenish, through yellow, apricot, pink to dark
reddish-brown, up to 2.2 cm long and 7 mm wide;
dorsal sepal free, or partly fused with the petals.
Petals red, lanceolate, free, up to 2 cm long and 6 mm
wide. Lip sessile, broadly oval-lanceolate, white to
pink, up to 2.5 cm long and 1 cm wide; disc pube-
scent. Column up to 1.5 cm long. (Fig. 11; Photo.
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Florida, the West Indies,
Mexico to northern South America.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Orange Walk, Belize
and Cayo Districts. Uncommon.
HABITAT. In open pastures, often on moist humus
on the ground, between tree roots or on old stumps.
FLOWERING SEASON. January to May. Flowers last
about two weeks.
EtymoLogY. From the Latin lanceolatus (nar-
rowed and tapered at both ends) in reference to the
leaf shape.

Plants terrestrial. Roots fasciculate, tuberous. Leaves
often absent when flowering spike produced, basal or
cauline, sessile. Stem erect, vaginate or bracteolate.
Inflorescences terminal, a subdense, many-flowered
raceme. Flowers large, often showy. Sepals free,
subsimilar, connivent; dorsal sepal concave; lateral
sepals decurrent on the column-foot forming a spur-
like extension. Petals joined to to dorsal sepal. Lip
sessile, arcuate. Column short, stout, basally ex-
tended in a long foot.
A genus of about 10 species native to the American
tropics and subtropics. One is known from Belize.
EtymoLoGY. From the Greek sakkos (a sack or
bag) and koilos (hollow) describing the spur-like
extension formed by the bases of the lateral sepals.

Plant terrestrial, a cluster of thickened, fleshy, tube-
rous roots. Leaves appear after the inflorescence has
faded, deciduous, usually up to 6-leaved in a rosette,
lanceolate, glossy, up to 20 cm long and 2.5 cm wide.
Inflorescence up to 50 cm tall, upright, flowers borne
on the upper third of a shortish brown peduncle with
white pubescence, with about 7 sheathing bracts
which are usually reddish in colour. Flowers numer-
ous, densely clustered, only opening slightly, up to 3
cm long with the ovary, not fragrant, white pube-
scent; ovary dark greenish-brown marked with three
paler lines leading to the base of each sepal, well
developed at flowering time. Sepals vary in colour
from greenish, through yellow, apricot, pink to dark
reddish-brown, up to 2.2 cm long and 7 mm wide;
dorsal sepal free, or partly fused with the petals.
Petals red, lanceolate, free, up to 2 cm long and 6 mm
wide. Lip sessile, broadly oval-lanceolate, white to
pink, up to 2.5 cm long and 1 cm wide; disc pube-
scent. Column up to 1.5 cm long. (Fig. 11; Photo.
23,24).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Florida, the West Indies,
Mexico to northern South America.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Orange Walk, Belize
and Cayo Districts. Uncommon.
HABITAT. In open pastures, often on moist humus
on the ground, between tree roots or on old stumps.
FLOWERING SEASON. January to May. Flowers last
about two weeks.
EtymoLogY. From the Latin lanceolatus (nar-
rowed and tapered at both ends) in reference to the
leaf shape.

Catling (1987b) studied the pollination mechan-

be both self-pollinated and hummingbird pollinated.
Plants terrestrial, or occasionally lithophytic,
glabrous or pubescent. Roots fleshy, tuberous. Leaves
rosulate, often variegated, may be petiolate, often
absent at time of flowering. Inflorescence erect, spi-
cate, laxly few- to many- flowered. Flowers small to
medium-sized, often glandular pubescent on outer
surface. Dorsal sepal and petals connivent, forming a
hood over the column; lateral sepals deflexed. Lip
sessile or clawed, often narrow, concave, enclosing
the column below. Column terete; rostellum biden-
tate.

Central America and South America. Three are
known from Belize.

Plant terrestrial, stout consisting of a rosette of leaves
arising from a cluster of very fleshy roots, pubescent.
Leaves basal, elliptic-oblong, tapering at both ends,
usually with silver stripes or spots, fasciculate, up to
25 cm long and 7 cm wide; long-petioled. Inflores-
cence apical, erect, spicate, loose-flowered of up to
15 flowers, up to 70 cm long; bracts lanceolate, up to
5.5 cm long. Flowers pleasantly lemon-scented,
yellowish-green, arcuate with dark green nerves, not
opening widely, up to 4 cm long; pedicellate ovary up
to 3 cm long, pubescent; floral bracts ovate-
lanceolate, up to 4 cm long. Sepals similar, pubescent
on the outside, up to 3.5 cm long and 0.8 cm wide;
lateral sepals horizontal or upcurved, undulate and
blunt. Petals hyaline, adnate with the dorsal sepal,
spathulate, up to 3 cm long and 0.5 cm wide. Lip
constricted near the apex with an expanded saggitate-
ovate mid-lobe and 2 long calli at the base, up to 4 cm
long and 1.1 cm wide. Column short, up to 2 cm long;
rostellum shallowly emarginate. (Fig. 12; Photo. 26)
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Belize, Guatemala, El
Salvador, Nicaragua and Panama.

S. acaulis has been reported by Spellman (1975)

been based on material of S. sceptrodes.
Small to medium-sized terrestrialherbs with fleshy
swollen roots. Leaves in a basal rosette, several.
Inflorescences erect, terminal, many-flowered, spi-
cate. Flowers usually arranged spirally, small, not
opening widely. Dorsal sepal free, adnate to the 2
petals forming a hood over the column. Lateral
sepals free, enclosing the base of the lip. Lip longer
than the other segments and envelloping the column
at the base. Column erect.
A genus of about 50 species with the majority in
the Americas. One is known from Belize.

lines.text: SUBTRIBE CRANICHIDINAE LINDL.
Terrestrial or epiphytic erect herbs. Roots clustered,
fleshy. Stems short. Leaves in a basal rosette, mem-
braneous, usually petiolate. Inflorescences terminal,
spicate, erect; peduncle with several sheaths.
Flowers few to many, in a raceme, rather small;
peduncle slender. Sepals and petals more or less
spreading, free; petals smaller than the sepals. Lip
uppermost in the flower, concave. Column short, with
a large rostellum; pollinia 2 but deeply divided; visci-
dium globose.
A genus of some 30 species, all native to the
American tropics and subtropics. One is known from
Belize.
ETymoLoGY. From the Greek kranos (helmet)
referring to the appearance of the concave lip.
Cranichis sylvatica A. Rich. & Gal. in Ann. Sc. Nat.
sér. 3(3): 30 (1845). Type: Mexico, A. Richard & H.
Galeotti (holo. P).
Cranichis pseudociliata Schltr. in Fedde, Repert. Sp.
Plant terrestrial, slender, up to 32 cm tall. Leaves 4-5,

SUBTRIBE HABENARIINAE BENTH.
Terrestrial herbs with one or more fleshy tuberoids
and fibrous roots. Stems erect, leafy or with leaves
only at, or near, the base. Leaves sheathing at the
base. Inflorescences terminal, 1- to many-flowered.
Flowers in a spike or raceme, usually green or white,
rarely showy. Dorsal sepal commonly erect and
hood-like. Lateral sepals spreading or reflexed.
Petals simple or bilobed. Lip simple or 3-lobed,
extended at the base into a spur; spur often long and
slender. Column very short; stigmas 2, stalked; rostel-
lum small, may be triangular, with divergent lateral
lobes; pollinia 2, clavate.
This is the largest genus of terrestrial orchids, with
about 600 species widely distributed in tropical and
subtropical parts of both the Old and New Worlds.
Thirteen are known from Belize, of which we have
seen eight.
Although generally inconspicuous, the flowers of
Habenaria are rather complex. In addition to the
petals and lip often being deeply divided, there are
two distinctly stalked stigmas at the base of the
column, and the viscidia (to which the pollinia are
attached) are often borne on long stalks derived from
the rostellum.
Most species of Habenaria are probably moth-
pollinated and, where the flowers have a fragrance,
this is generally most noticeable at night.
EtymoLogY. From the Latin habena (reins)
referring to the divisions of the petals and lip which,
in manyspecies, are strap-like.

SUBTRIBE CRANICHIDINAE LINDL.
Terrestrial or epiphytic erect herbs. Roots clustered,
fleshy. Stems short. Leaves in a basal rosette, mem-
braneous, usually petiolate. Inflorescences terminal,

Plant terrestrial, rather slender, up to 85 cm tall, with
an ovoid tuberoid at the base. Stem leafy. Leaves
more or less spreading, lanceolate to oblong-elliptic,
pale to rather dark green, often with a darker mid-
stripe, up to 15 cm long and 3.2 cm wide; two basal
sheaths. Inflorescence loosely many-flowered, up to
30 cm long. Flowers fragrant, yellowish-green with
pale green sepals; pedicellate ovaries up to 2 cm long.
Sepals concave; dorsal sepal keeled, up to 6.5 mm
long and 6 mm wide; lateral sepals reflexed, up to 8
mm long and 5 mm wide. Petals erect, more or less
oblong, shallowly 3-toothed at the apex, with a tooth
on the lower margin at the base, up to 6 mm long and
2 mm wide. Lip decurved, linear, with a tooth at each
side at the base, up to 1.1 cm long and 2 mm wide;
spur slender, pale green, up to 3 cm long. Column
stout. (Fig. 16; Photo. 30).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Florida, the West Indies,
Mexico to Brazil, Peru and Paraguay.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Orange Walk and Bel-
ize Districts. Uncommon.
HABITAT. In swampy woodland below 100m.
FLOWERING SEASON. December and January.
Flowers last about three weeks.
ETymoLoGY. From the Latin floribundus (profu-
sely flowering).
NoTE. The scent of these flowers resembles that of
honeysuckle.
6. Habenaria lankesteri Ames, Sched. Orch. 4: 2
(1923). Type: Costa Rica, Jocosal, C. H. Lankester
342 (holo. AMES, photo. of holo. K!; iso. K!).
Plant terrestrial, up to 18 cm tall. Leaves appro-
ximate, basal, elliptic-oblong, acuminate, up to 5 cm
long and 7 mm wide. Inflorescence racemose with 5
or more flowers, pedicel short; floral bracts up to 1
cm long, lanceolate, appressed to ovary. Flowers
green. Lateral sepals pendent, ovate, fleshy, concave,
up to 4 mm long and 2 mm wide; dorsal sepal
elliptic-ovate, erect, up to 4 mm long. Petals
triangular-oblong, fleshy, up to 3.5 mm long and 1.5
mm wide. Lip fleshy, 3-lobed with lateral lobes
shorter than mid-lobe, up to 4 mm long; spur pendent,
slender, up to 1 cm long.
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Belize and Costa Rica.
17 Habenaria
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Cayo District (Moun-
tain Pine Ridge Reserve). Rare.
HABITAT. In open grassland.
FLOWERING SEASON. Not known.
ETymoLoGY. Named after Charles Herbert Lan-
kester (1879-1969), an English coffee planter and
plant collector.
NoTES. Reported by Standley and Record (1936)
and otherwise known only from Costa Rica. H. lanke-
steri is apparently allied to H. repens but differs in the
shape of the petals and lip.
7. Habenaria mesodactyla Griseb., Fl. Brit. W.

Plant terrestrial, very slender, up to 50 cm tall, with
two small tuberoids at the base. Stem leafy. Leaves
few, erect and clasping the stem, linear- lanceolate to
linear, attenuate, up to 8 cm long and 4.5 mm wide.
Inflorescence loosely 2- to 6-flowered, up to 12 cm
long. Flowers small and inconspicuous, yellowish-
green with green sepals; pedicellate ovaries erect,
somewhat incurved, ribbed, about 1.7 cm long.
Sepals concave, with minutely ciliate margins; dorsal
sepal up to 5.5 mm long and 4 mm wide; lateral
sepals spreading, keeled, with the apex of the keel
extended into a point, up to 7 mm long and 2.5 mm
wide. Petals deeply bilobed; upper lobe incurved,
often connivent with the dorsal sepal, up to 5 mm
long and 0.7 mm wide; lower lobe upcurved, very
slender, up to 8 mm long. Lip 3-lobed almost to the
base; lateral lobes curved in towards the mid-lobe,
commonly slender, up to 1 cm long; mid-lobe linear,
up to 6 mm long and 0.7 mm wide; spur often
upcurved, slender, pale green, somewhat swollen
towards the apex, up to 1.2 cm long. (Fig. 17H;
Photo. 31).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Belize, northern South
America and Trinidad.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Belize, Cayo, Stann
Creek and Toledo Districts. Locally common.
HABITAT. In savannah and open pine-ridge, from 0
FLOWERING SEASON. July to October. Flowers last
about three weeks.
EtymoLogY. From the Greek meso (middle) and
dactyl (finger).
NoTEs. These are extremely inconspicuous plants
that are easily overlooked. Collections referrable to
this species were the basis of Correll's report (1965)
of H. leprieurii Rchb. f.

Plant terrestrial, up to 65 cm tall with an oblong or
ellipsoid tuberoid at base. Stem leafy. Leaves several,
ascending, concentrated towards the middle of the
stem, lanceolate to linear, somewhat folded length-
wise, up to 18 cm long and 1.4 cm wide. Inflores-
cence rather densely many-flowered, up to 24 cm
long. Flowers fragrant, yellowish-green with green
sepals; pedicellate ovaries up to 1.3 cm long. Sepals
concave; dorsal sepal up to 6 mm long and 4.5 mm
wide; lateral sepals somewhat reflexed, up to 7 mm
long and 3 mm wide. Petals bilobed, almost to the
base; upper lobe connivent with the dorsal sepal,
about 5 mm long and 1 mm wide; lower lobe
spreading-upcurved, very slender, up to 9 mm long.

diverging, upcurved, very slender, up to 1.1 cm long;
mid-lobe linear, up to 7 mm long and 0.7 mm wide;
spur slender, pale green, up to 1.2 cm long. (Fig.
16K).

can tropics and subtropics.

and Toledo Districts. Uncommon.

12. Habenaris rodeiensis Barb. Rodr., Gen. Sp.

Plant terrestrial, rather slender, up to 48 cm tall, with
a tuberoid at the base. Stem leafy. Leaves several,
erect and clasping the stem, narrowly lanceolate,
glaucous, up to 9 cm long and 1.3 cm wide. Inflores-
cence commonly about 10- to 12-flowered, up to 11
cm long. Flowers fragrant, often more or less cleisto-
gamous; pedicellate ovaries up to 3.2 cm long. Sepals
pale green with darker green veins, concave, up to 1.2
cm long; dorsal sepal up to 4 mm wide; lateral sepal
up to 3 mm wide. Petals deeply bilobed, greenish-
white, up to 1 cm long; upper lobe connivent with the
dorsal sepal, up to 4.5 mm long and 2.5 mm wide;
lower lobe upcurved, slender, up to 2 mm long. Lip
deeply 3-lobed, pale green with a white base, up to
1.4 cm long; lateral lobes diverging, up to 3 mm long
and 0.8 mm wide; mid-lobe linear, up to 4 mm long
and 1.2 mm wide; spur slender, pale green with a
white base, up to 3.8 cm long. (Fig. 17G; Photo. 35).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Belize, Venezuela and
Brazil.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Cayo District (Moun-
tain Pine Ridge Reserve). Uncommon.
HABITAT. On well-drained slopes in open pine-
ridge between 700 and 1000m.
FLOWERING SEASON. Throughout the year, flow-
ering having been recorded in April, July, October
and December. Flowers open, or at least mature, from
the base of the raceme and individually last only a
few days.
ETymoLoGY. From Rodeio, in Brazil, where the
type specimen was found.
NoTEs. The short-lived and often more or less
cleistogamous flowers are a distinctive feature of the
Belize population. H. rodeiensis was not known from
anywhere in Central America prior to our collections
which were previouslyreported,incorrectly, as H.
leprieurii Rchb. f.

Plant terrestrial, up to 50 cm tall, with an ovoid
tuberoid at base. Stem leafy. Leaves few, more or less
erect, often clasping the stem, elliptic-lanceolate.
acuminate, up to 11 cm long and 1.4 cm wide;
sheaths on the lower part of the stem veined and
spotted with dark brown. Inflorescence 1-or 2-
flowered. Flowers greenish-cream with green sepals;
pedicellate ovaries erect, somewhat curved, ribbed,
up to 9 cm long. Sepals concave; dorsal sepal up to
1.2 cm long and 8 mm wide; lateral sepals reflexed,
acute, up to 1.4 cm long and 6 mm wide. Petals
bilobed almost to the base; upper lobe connivent with
the dorsal sepal, up to 1.2 cm long and 4 mm wide;
lower lobe spreading- upcurved, up to 1 cm long and
1.5 cm wide. Lip 3-lobed to the base, rather fleshy,
with the lobes all more or less linear and up to 1.4 cm
long and 3 mm wide; lateral lobes diverging; spur
pale green, slender at base, somewhat swollen to-
wards the apex, up to 6 cm long. (Fig. 17; Photo. 36).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Mexico to Brazil and
Argentina.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Belize, Cayo ( Moun-
tain Pine Ridge Reserve) and Toledo Districts.
Locally common.
HABITAT. On stony or sandy soils in open pine-
ridge between 50 and 1000m.
FLOWERING SEASON. June to September, and
January.
EtymoLogY. From the Latin trifida (divided into
three) in reference to the lip shape.

lines.text: TRIBE TRIPHOREAE DRESSLER
18. Psilochilus Barb. Rodr.
Terrestrial or epiphytic, plants with creeping rhi-
zomes. Roots adventitious, fleshy. Leaves membrana-
ceous with lax petioles. Inflorescences terminal, a
short spicate raceme. Flowers few. Sepals free,
keeled along the mid-vein. Petals free, not keeled
along mid-vein. Lip free, 3-lobed; disc with 3 longi-
tudinal calli. Column elongate, clavate; anther ter-
minal, 2-celled, mobile; pollinia 4.
This is a monotypic genus of tropical America.
EtymoLogY. From the Greek psilo (smooth) and
chilus (lipped) in reference to the appearance of the
lip.
Psilochilus macrophyllus (Lindl.) Ames, Orch.
Fasc. 7: 45 (1922). Type: locality unknown, Linden
(holo. K-LINDL.!).
Pogonia macrophylla Lindl. in Ann. Mag. Nat. Hist.
P. physurifolia Rchb. f. in Nederl. Kruidk. Arch. 4:
Plant terrestrial or epiphytic, with fleshy roots. Stem
branched, ascending. Leaves rigid, membranaceous,
oval-elliptic, up to 8 cm long and 5 cm wide. Inflores-
cence terminal, racemose, 1- to 2-flowered; bracts
leafy, up to 2 cm long and 1.5 cm wide. Flowers
ringent with greenish sepals, greenish- white petals
and white lip. Sepals stiff and fleshy; dorsal sepal up
to 1.9 cm long and 3 mm wide; lateral sepals up to 1.8
cm long and 3 mm wide. Petals thinner than the
sepals, up to 1.8 cm long and 3 mm wide. Lip
3-lobed, up to 1.6 cm long and 8 mm wide; lateral
lobes acute; mid-lobe with serrate margins. Column
with 2 conspicuous broad apical teeth on the side of
the rostellum. (Fig. 18).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. The West Indies, Central
America to Panama.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Cayo, Stann Creek and
Toledo Districts. Uncommon.
HABITAT. On leaf litter over sandy soil on the
forest floor and on mossy tree branches about 3 m
above the ground.
FLOWERING SEASON. December.
ETymoLoGY. From the Greek macrophyllus
(large-leaved).
NoTE. Reported by Catling & Catling (1988).

SUBTRIBE VANILLINAE LINDL.
19. Epistephium Kunth
Terrestrial herbs. Stems tall, simple or branched. Lea-
ves chartaceous to coriaceous, usually sessile or
cordate-clasping, strongly veined. Inflorescences ter-
minal or, rarely, axillary, racemose, many-flowered.
Flowers large; bracts short; apex of ovary with an
urceolate cup. Sepals subequal, free. Petals rather
similar to sepals but sometimes larger. Lip adnate to
the column, obovate, simple or slightly 3-lobed, en-
clasping the base of the column. Column long, dilated
above, broadly 3-lobed at apex. Capsule oblong-
cylindric.
A genus of about 20 species known from Belize,
Trinidad and northern South America. One is known
from Belize.
ETyMoLoGY. From the Greek epi (upon, above)
and stefos (a crown, wreath) in reference to the
crown-like growth that remains at the apex of the
ovary.

A genus of about 60 or more species distributed
widely throughout the tropics. Three are known from
Belize.
In its climbing habit Vanilla is comparable with
Vanda and its allies, but is easily distinguished by the
adventitious roots borne at each node opposite the
leaf. These roots are the main supporting organs of
the plant and grow very long, branching freely when
near the ground (Bechtel et al., 1992).
Vanilla was first used by the Aztecs of Mexico to
give flavour and aroma to beverages made from
cocoa. The first true pictorial representation of an
orchid in the New World was in the famous Codex
Badianus which contained drawings and texts pre-
pared by a Mexican Indian in 1552. The drawing of a
vanilla plant was named tlilxochitl, in the Náhuatl
language, meaning "black flower' in reference to the
fruits (Escobar, 1990-1992).

pod) referring to the long, slender pod.

GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Florida, the West Indies,
Central America to northern South America. V. plani-
folia is widely cultivated throughout the tropics to
provide commercial vanilla essence.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Belize, Cayo, Stann
Creek and Toledo Districts. Rare.
HABITAT. Climbing on trees in moist to wet for-
est.
FLOWERING SEASON. April. Flowers last one to
two weeks.
ETymoLoGY. From the Latin plani (flat) and folia
(leaved) in reference to the leaf shape.
NOTES. A specimen, from Stann Creek District,
previously identified as V. pomposa Schiede, has
been reidentified as V. planifolia (Catling & Catling
1988). Although formerly widespread in semi-
evergreen forests throughout Belize V. planifolia has
become one of the first casualties of deforestation.
Terrestrial or epiphytic herbs. Stems fleshy, often
pseudobulbous. Leaves few, sheathing at the base.
Inflorescences terminal, erect. Flowers commonly
small, few to many in a raceme. Sepals and petals
spreading; petals narrow. Lip simple or 3-lobed, with
or without a basal callus. Column elongate, strongly
curved; pollinia 4, ovoid, waxy.
A large genus of about 200 species, widely distri-
buted in both tropical and temperate regions of the
world and closely allied to Malaxis. One is known
from Belize.

shining) referring to the glossy leaves of the type
species, L. loeselii (L.) L.C. Rich.

EtymoLogY. From the Latin elatus (tall) in refer-
ence to the elevated superior inflorescence.
NOTES. There has been some confusion about the
correct nomenclature of this plant. A complete re-
view of the species was made by Garay & Sweet
(1974) who considered this species to be widespread
in the tropics and subtropics of both the New and Old
World. The earliest name for this species then is L
nervosa. Atwood (1974), Hamer (1974, 1982-1984)
and Adams (1984) follow Garay for the American
plant, whereas Catling & Catling (1988) considered
the American species to be distinct from the Old
World one and used the name L elata Lindl. Al-
though rare in the Orchidaceae such disjuncts are
known (eg, Polystachya concreta (Jacq.) Garay &
Sweet and Eulophia alta (L.) Fawc. & Rendle). We
follow Catling & Catling, who prefer to distinguish
the American plant from the Asian.

23. Eulophia R.Br. ex Lindl.
Terrestrial or rarely epiphytic herbs. Rhizome stout,
in the tropical Americas always with corm-like an-
nual segments. Leaves several, from the apex of the
corm, usually plicate, sheathing at the base.
Inflorescences from the base of the corm, erect,
single or, rarely, branching. Flowers small to large
and showy. Sepals spreading to reflexed. Petals often
more or less erect. Lip joined to the column foot,
3-lobed, commonly crested, pouch-like or spurred at
the base. Column basally extended into a foot; polli-
nia 2, often deeply cleft, waxy.
A large genus of over 200 species, widespread in
the tropics but most numerous in Africa. One is
known from Belize.
EtymoLogY. From the Greek eu (well) and lo-
phos (plume) referring to the crested lip.
Eulophia alta (L) Fawc. & Rendle, Fl. Jamaica 1:
112 (1910). Type: based on Plumier's 'Limodorum

Dendrobium longifolium Kunth, Nov. Gen. & Sp. 1:
Eulophia longifolia (Kunth) Schltr. in Orchideen:
Plant terrestrial, large, erect, up to 1.5 m tall. Corms
up to 6 cm in diameter. Leaves linear-elliptic, promi-
nently veined, acuminate, up to 1.2m long and 8 cm
wide. Inflorescence from the base of the corm, loose-
ly many-flowered; peduncle stout, up to 1 m long and
1.2 cm in diameter, provided with several large
sheaths. Flowers in a raceme; pedicellate ovaries
slender, up to 2.5 cm long. Sepals brownish-green,
keeled, up to 7 mm wide above the middle; dorsal
sepal up to 2.1 cm long; lateral sepals joined to the
sides of the column-foot and directed upwards, up to
2.4 cm long. Petals curved over the column, greenish
suffused with maroon, up to 1.7 cm long and 8 mm
wide. Lip pouch-like at the base, up to 1.9 cm long
and 1.7 cm across the lateral lobes when spread, with
two erect flap-like projections below the middle;
lateral lobes erect, greenish suffused with maroon,
rounded at the apex; mid-lobe decurved, maroon,
with undulate margins and several rows of papillae
along the veins. Column curved, green, with a broad
maroon foot, up to 9 mm long. (Fig. 23; Photo. 43).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Throughout the Ameri-
can tropics and subtropics, as well as Central and
West Africa.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Orange Walk, Cayo,
Stann Creek and Toledo Districts. Locally common.
HABITAT. In more or less open areas up to 200 m.
It favours heavy, moisture-retentive soils and often
found along roadsides or on cleared land reverting to
bush.
FLOWERING SEASON. September to February.
Flowers last up to a month.
EtymoLoGY. From the Latin altus (tall) in refer-
ence to the size of the plant.
NOTES. Although large, non-flowering plants are
easily overlooked as they greatly resemble the seed-
lings of various palms. The leaves die down during,
or soon after, the flowering period and the new shoot
is produced about May (the end of the dry season).
The separate inflorescence does not appear until Sep-
tember or October but then develops rapidly.

can tropics and subtropics.

tricts. Apparently not previously recorded from Bel-
ize despite being frequent along the Western High-
way between Belize City and Belmopan. Locally
common.

pine-ridge below 100 m. Frequently growing in asso-

trees or stumps.

about two weeks.

new shoot develops with the inflorescence. It is
known as the 'Cow Horn' orchid in Florida.

plicate, prominently veined. Inflorescences from the

Plant usually epiphytic, erect, up to 80 cm tall. Pseu-

and 4 cm in diameter. Leaves 2 to 3, broadly lanceo-
late, strongly veined, acuminate, rigid, leathery,
shortly petiolate, up to 40 cm long and 8 cm wide.

fragrant; pedicellate ovaries up to 4 cm long. Sepals
and petals yellow, suffused with maroon at the mar-
gins, up to 2.2 cm long and 9 mm wide; sepals
concave. Lip 3-lobed, hinged to the column-foot, up
to 1.8 cm long and 1.1 cm wide when spread; lateral
lobes rounded, yellowish, suffused and veined with
purple; mid-lobe spreading, emarginate or 2-lobed at
the apex, white with purple spots; callus of 2 pairs of
erect fleshy keels with 2 separate teeth in front.

A genus of about 50 species, all native to the
American tropics. One is known from Belize.
Pollinated by male perfume-collecting bees which
are attracted by the strong musky odour, emitted by
the male flowers, a few days after opening. The
antennae, at the base of the column, are an important
part of the pollination mechanism, triggering an
explosive release of the pollinia when touched by the
visiting bees (van der Pijl & Dodson, 1966).
The unisexual flowers of this genus, and the clo-
sely related Cycnoches, are unique in the orchid
family. They are also unusual in being dimorphic, the
separate male and female flowers differing to varying
degrees in appearance.
ETymoLoGY. From the Greek kata (down) and
seta (bristle), referring to the antenna-like append-
ages at the base of the column of the male flower.
Catasetum integerrimum Hook. in Bot. Mag. 67:
t.3823 (1841). Type: Guatemala, Ure Skinner s.n.
(holo.K!).
Catasetum maculatum auct. non Kunth.
Plant epiphytic or lithophytic, stout, erect, up to 80
cm tall. Roots numerous with many ascending often
forming a nest-like mass. Pseudobulbs conical-
fusiform, up to 25 cm long and 5 cm in diameter,
covered by scarious leaf-sheaths when young. Leaves
distichous, elliptic to oblong-elliptic, abruptly
pointed, with undulate margins, up to 60 cm long and
12 cm wide, sheaths papery, spine-tipped after the
leaves fall. Inflorescence several-flowered, up to 45
or rarely 60 cm long; peduncle stout and glaucous.
Flowers with the lip uppermost in both sexes; pedi-
cellate ovaries S-shaped, up to 4.5 cm long. Male
flowers somewhat variable in colour. Sepals and
petals descending, greenish,usually more or less
spotted or suffused with purple, up to 3.2 cm wide;
sepals incurved, concave, up to 5.5 cm long; petals
convex, upcurved at the tip, up to 5.2 cm long. Lip
fleshy, saccate, margins ciliate towards base, rigid,
yellowish-green, prominently veined or spotted with-
in, up to 3 cm long and 2.3 cm wide. Column with a
beak-like apex, up to 4 cm long; antennae up to 2.5
cm long. Female flowers greenish or yellowish-
green. Sepals spreading, up to 1.5 cm wide; dorsal
sepal concave, up to 2.5 cm long; lateral sepals
incurved above the middle, up to 3.5 cm long. Petals
recurved, convex, up to 2.8 cm long and 1.7 cm wide.
Lip broadly calceolate,rigid, prominently veined
28 Clowesia
within, up to 3.5 cm long and 3.3 cm wide. Column
stout, up to 1.5 cm long. (Fig. 27; Photo. 47, 48).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Mexico to Nicaragua.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Orange Walk, Belize,
Cayo, Stann Creek and Toledo Districts. Common.
HABITAT. On trees and stumps in many situations
and at all altitudes. Sometimes also on fence posts,
rocks and buildings. Often seen on palms, particu-
larly coconut and cohune (Orbignya cohune (Mart.)
Dahl.).
FLOWERING SEASON. June to November. Flowers
last about a week.
EtymoLoGY. From the Latin integerrimus (abso-
lutely undivided, entire) in reference to the fact that
the mouth of the lip is circular, contracted and entire.
NoTEs. Among the most common and widely
distributed of the larger orchids in Belize and remark-
able in its adaptability to a variety of unusual habitats.
The numerous ascending roots function as debris
collectors and thus have an important role in ensuring
the plant has an adequate supply of mineral nutrients.
Leaves are deciduous by about February and new
shoots appear at the end of the season.
According to Halcrow & Halcrow (1967) it is
sometimes known as the 'Pipe Orchid'.
Usually epiphytic herbs with short stems. Pseudo-
bulbs fleshy, ovoid to fusiform, several-noded,
covered with leaf-sheaths when young. Leaves large,
plicate and articulated to a leaf-sheath, deciduous.
Inflorescences from the basal nodes of the pseudo-
bulb, pendent, racemose, several-flowered. Flowers
complex, showy, membranous, bisexual. Sepals and
petals free, petals often broader and may be fringed.
Lip free from the column, saccate or spurred, apex
fringed, denticulate or entire. Column short to fairly
long, without antennae at base; pollinia 2, large,
sulcate; stipe 1, tensioned; viscidium large, released
by pressure on the stipe.
The genus Clowesia was established by John Lind-
ley in 1843. Most authors have treated Clowesia as a
section of Catasetum until 1975, when C. Dodson
resurrected the genus. Clowesia is distinguished rea-
dily from Catasetum by having bisexual flowers, a lip
that is free from the column and by its pollination
mechanism which involves the downward rotation if
the viscidium when pressure is applied to the pollina-
rium (Bechtel et al., 1992).
There are five species distributed from Mexico to
Venezuela. One is known from Belize.
EtymoLoGY. Named after the Rev. John Clowes, a

29 Cycnoches
Plants frequently produce both male and female
flowers but usually in separate racemes and at differ-
ent times. Mixed racemes and hermaphrodite flowers
occasionally occur. In both this genus and Catase-
tum, light intensity has been shown to influence sex
expression (Gregg, 1975). Plants in full sunlight are
more likely to produce female inflorescences than
those growing in shade.
The pollination mechanism involves a bee, from
the genus Euglossa, landing on the lip of a male
flower. The lip, which has a flexible claw, swings
down under the weight of the bee, causing the bee's
abdomen to touch the anther-cap, which discharges
the pollinia. When the bee then visits a female flower
it lands on the lip, attracted by the odour located at the
apex of the column, and when dropping off, the
pollinia are caught by the finger-like rostellar pro-
cesses of the column (van de Pijl & Dodson, 1966).
ETYmoLoGY. From the Greek kyknos (swan) and
auchen (neck) referring to the slender, curved column
of the male flower.

raceme, medium sized to large, unisexual and dimor-
phic. Sepals and petals similar. Lip uppermost in the
flower, simple or variously lobed. Column stout or
slender, curved, more or less club- shaped; pollinia 2,
waxy, ovoid, sulcate.
A genus of about 12 species, all in the American
tropics. Two are known from Belize. They are com-
monly known as 'swan orchids'.

sickly-sweet fragrance
29 Cycnoches
Plants frequently produce both male and female
flowers but usually in separate racemes and at differ-
ent times. Mixed racemes and hermaphrodite flowers
occasionally occur. In both this genus and Catase-
tum, light intensity has been shown to influence sex
expression (Gregg, 1975). Plants in full sunlight are
more likely to produce female inflorescences than
those growing in shade.
The pollination mechanism involves a bee, from
the genus Euglossa, landing on the lip of a male
flower. The lip, which has a flexible claw, swings
down under the weight of the bee, causing the bee's
abdomen to touch the anther-cap, which discharges
the pollinia. When the bee then visits a female flower
it lands on the lip, attracted by the odour located at the
apex of the column, and when dropping off, the
pollinia are caught by the finger-like rostellar pro-
cesses of the column (van de Pijl & Dodson, 1966).
ETYmoLoGY. From the Greek kyknos (swan) and
auchen (neck) referring to the slender, curved column
of the male flower.

2. Cycnoches ventricosum Batem., Orch. Mex.
Guat.: t. 5 (1837). Type: Guatemala, Ure Skinner s.n.
(holo. K!).
Plant epiphytic, stout, erect or spreading, up to 60 cm
tall. Pseudobulbs up to 30 cm long and 4 cm in
diameter though commonly less. Leaves elliptic to
narrowly oblanceolate, acuminate, up to 45 cm long
and 10 cm wide. Male inflorescence arching, several-
flowered, up to 40 cm long. Flowers fragrant. Sepals
and petals yellowish-green; dorsal sepal spreading,
up to 7 cm long and 1.6 cm wide; lateral sepals and
petals reflexed, up to 6 cm long and 2.2 cm wide. Lip
lanceolate-elliptic above an elongate slender base,
markedly convex, creamy white, shading to pale
green at the apex, fleshy, with a dark green basal
patch around a small callus, up to 5 cm long and 1.8
cm wide. Column slender, up to 4 cm long. Female
inflorescence erect or spreading, commonly 1-or
2-flowered, up to 14 cm long. Flowers heavily fra-
grant, similar to the male flowers. Sepals up to 2.4 cm
wide. Petals up to 2.8 cm wide. Column stout, about 2
cm long. (Fig. 30; Photo. 51, 52).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Mexico to Panama.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Cayo, Stann Creek and
Toledo Districts. Uncommon.
HABITAT. On trees, stumps and rotten logs in
moist broad-leaved forest, pastures and orchards be-
tween 50 and 150 m.
PLOWERING SEASON. July to February. Male
flowers last about a week, female flowers up to three
weeks. Plants lose their leaves during the winter
months and will occasionally flower when leafless.
EtymoLogY. from the Latin ventricosus (bellied
out below, distended, expanded) in reference to the
lip shape.
NoTEs. Material illustrated by Halcrow & Hal-
crow (1967) under the name C. warscewiczii appears
to represent the first record of this species in Belize.
C. warscewiczii Rchb. f., which is very closely
30 Mormodes
related to C. ventricosum, is probably restricted to
Costa Rica and Panama and differs in the slender
basal portion of the lip (claw) being shorter and the
callus being more protruberant.
Another closely allied species, C. chlorochilon
Klotzsch, was included by Spellman et al. (1975) on
their checklist of Belize monocotyledons. In this
case, the known distribution is northern South Amer-
ica and the lip is oblong-elliptic with virtually no
claw, quite unlike anything we have seen. Allen
(1952) treated both C. warscewiczii and C. chlorochi-
lon as varieties of C. ventricosum.
Epiphytic or terrestrial herbs. Pseudobulbs oblong,
Heshy, several-leaved. Leaves distichous, elongate,
plicate. Inflorescences lateral, 1 to several, from the
nodes of the pseudobulbs, racemose. Flowers showy,
often polymorphic. Sepals and petals free, spreading
or reflexed. Lip entire, 3-lobed, hairless or slightly
hairy; side lobes reflexed; mid-lobe apiculate. Col-
umn thick, erect, twisted to one side in male flowers;
pollinia 4, waxy, oblong.
A genus of about 20 species in Central and South
America. Two are known from Belize.
The pollination mechanism of the genus Mor-
modes is interesting (van der Pijl & Dodson, 1966).
Male euglossine bees, attracted by the flower's
odour, land on the lip and disturb the apex of the
column, which is twisted. The anther-cap acts as a
hinge and swings the pollinaria up onto the bee's
back. The stipe, which is coiled at this stage, gradual-
ly uncurls, and, after about thirty minutes, is in the
correct position to be placed on the stigma.
ETyMoLoGY. From the Greek mormo (phantom)
and eides (looking like) referring to the grotesque
appearance of the flowers.

strongly veined. Petals linear, up to 3 cm long and 1.2
cm wide. Lip fleshy, folded and twisted, interior
chocolate-brown within and strongly veined, pink on

from the nodes of the pseudobulbs, racemose,
several-flowered, up to 50 cm long; peduncle slender;
bracts ovate, up to 0.7 cm long. Flowers variable.
Sepals and petals fleshy, green, yellowish or maroon,
marked with purple-brown;
lanceolate, acute, up to 13.5 cm long and 11.2 cm
wide; petals elliptic-lanceolate, acute, up to 3.2 cm
long and 1.3 cm wide. Lip reddish-brown, greenish-

lobed, pubescent, up to 3 cm long; side lobes twisted,
up to 1.5 cm long. Column somewhat twisted, ar-
cuate, up to 2.7 cm long.
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Mexico, Belize and
Peru.

known.
HABITAT. Epiphytic.
FLOWERING SEASON. Not known.
ETymoLoGY. Named after Joseph Warscewicz
(1812-1866), a Lithuanian-born gardener and plant

SUBTRIBE CRYPTARRHENINAE DRESSLER
Small epiphytic herbs. Rhizome short. Stems short,
sometimes pseudobulbous, usually concealed by
overlapping leaf-sheaths. Leaves somewhat leathery
or fleshy. Inflorescences from a leaf-axil or the base
of the pseudobulb, few-to many-flowered. Flowers
in a raceme, small. Sepals and petals similar, spread-
ing. Lip 3-lobed above a narrow base, often more or
less anchor-shaped, with a basal callus. Column
short, dilated above, lacking wings or a foot; pollinia
4 in pairs, waxy.
There are probably four species, widespread in the
American tropics. Two are known from Belize but
we have seen only one.
The genus Cryptarrhena was reviewed by R.L
Dressler (1980).
ETYmoLoGY. From the Greek kryptos (hidden)
and arrhen (stamen) referring to the hood-like clinan-
drium which covers the anther.

wide;

wide;
lateral sepals oblique. Petals elliptic-
