Plant epiphytic, small, hanging, without pseudo-
bulbs. Stem several, flattened, up to 21 cm long.
Leaves deciduous, numerous, distichous, pale green,
up to 4 cm long and 6 mm wide and about 6 mm
apart; leaf sheaths green, clasping and concealing the
stem, becoming brown and papery after the leaves
fall; rarely, a short aerial root is produced from the
base of the leaf-sheath. Inflorescence from base of
leaf-sheath; pedicel up to 1.7 cm long, partly
enclosed by leaf-sheath. Flowers single, not opening
fully, cream- coloured, not fragrant; sepals, petals and
lip spotted with purple, particularly on inner surface;
ovary up to 4 mm in diameter, subtended by numer-
ous translucent hair-like projections. Dorsal sepal up
to 5 mm long and 2 mm wide; lateral sepals up to 7
mm long and 2.5 mm wide, curving inwards. Petals
up to 4 mm long and 1.5 mm long, curving inwards.
Lip triangular-saggitate, smooth, up to 5 mm long and
6 mm wide, curved inwards. Column with a short
foot. (Fig. 33L).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Belize, Nicaragua to Pa-
nama, and Venezuela, Surinam and Brazil.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Toledo District. Rare.
HABITAT. On trees in dense wet forest.
FLOWERING SEASON. September and October.
Flowers last seven to ten days.
EymoLogY. From the Greek brachy (short) and
poda (foot) in reference to the short column-foot.
NOTE. D. brachypoda is almost indistinguishable
vegatatively from D. panamensis but can be iden-
tified by the numerous hair-like projections on the
ovary.

flattened, with a narrow base and two slender
backward-directed lateral lobes. Column long for the
flower, up to 4 mm long. (Fig. 33K; Photo. 56).

Plant epiphytic, small, creeping to hanging, often in
clumps. Stems freely to densely branched, leafy
throughout and concealed by the imbricating leaf-
sheaths, up to 12 cm long and 1.5 mm in diameter.
Leaves distichous, persistent, prominently hairy
along the margins, dark green with a prominent mid-
vein beneath, 2-2.5 mm apart, up to 9 mm long
(including the sheath), blade up to 6 mm long and 2
mm wide. Inflorescence 1-flowered, from the axils of
the upper leaves; peduncle very slender, up to 6 mm
long. Flower not obviously scented, small, scarcely
opening, greenish-yellow; ovary covered in white
fleshy hairs and partly hidden by a small bract. Sepals
and petals similar, pale green, up to 5.5 mm long and
2.5 mm wide. Lip whitish with a slight purple suffu-
sion, incurved, more or less anchor-shaped when
flattened, with a narrow base and two slender
backward-directed lateral lobes. Column long for the
flower, up to 4 mm long. (Fig. 33K; Photo. 56).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Cuba, the West Indies,
Belize to Honduras, and Costa Rica.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Toledo District. Rare.
HABITAT. On trees in wet evergreen forest.
FLOWERING SEASON. September and October.
EtymologY. From the Greek hystrix (a por-
cupine).
5. Dichaea muricatoides Hamer & Garay in Hamer,
Orquid. El. Salvador 1: 148 (1974). Type: Guate-
mala, H. von Türckheim (holo. BT).
Dichaea türckheimii Kraenzl. in Pflanzenr. 4, 50
(Heft. 83): 39 (1923), not Schltr. 1916.
D. muricata var. muricata (Sw.) Lindl., Gen. Sp.
Orch. Pl.: 209 (1833).
Plant epiphytic, tufted, pendant, growing in clumps.
Stem simple or branched, compressed, concealed by
leaf-sheaths, up to 60 cm long; aerial roots may be
produced from the leaf bases anywhere along the
stem. Leaves distichous, persistent, about 7 mm
apart, with imbricating leaf-sheaths, olive green, up
to 2 cm long and 7 mm wide. Inflorescence 1-
32 Dichaea
flowered, produced from the axil of the leaves to-
wards the end of the stem. Flowers on slender
peduncle of up to 1 cm long, slightly fragrant, up to
1.8 cm in diameter; ovary muricate, about 1 mm long.
Sepals and petals similar; sepals orange, up to 1.4 cm
long and 4.5 mm wide; petals pale orange spotted
with reddish-purple, up to 1.2 cm long and 4 mm
wide. Lip blue-purple,incurved, saggitate, with 2
lateral lobes arrising from the middle of the lip, up to
8 mm long. Column short, fleshy, up to 3.5 mm long.
(Fig. 33; Photo. 57).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. The West Indies, Me-
xico to northern South America.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Cayo (including the
Mountain Pine Ridge Reserve) and Toledo Districts.
Uncommon.
HABITAT. On trees in wet forest, often near rivers.
FLOWERING SEASON. July to October. Flowers last
a few days.
ETymoLoGY. In reference to the similarity to D.
muricata using the Greek suffix -oides (indicating a
resemblance to).
NoTE. Previously reported as D. muricata (Sw.)
Lindl. from which it differs in having larger leaves
and slightly larger flowers.
6. Dichaea muricata (Sw.) Lindl., Gen. Sp. Orch.
Pl.: 209 (1833). Type: Jamaica, Swartz (holo. S).
var. neglecta (Schltr.) Kraenzl. in Engler, Das
Pflanzenr. 4, 50: Heft. 83: 38 (1923). Type: Mexico,
Schiede 1053 (holo. Bt).
Dichaea neglecta Schltr. in Beih. Bot. Centralbl. 36:
420 (1918).
Plant epiphytic, often adhering to tree trunk, tufted.
Stem branched, compressed, concealed by leaf-
sheaths, up to 20 cm long and 2.5 mm in diameter;
aerial roots produced freely along the stem. Leaves
dictichous, persistent, elliptic, spreading, usually
about 4-5 mm apart; leaf-sheaths clasping the stem,
spotted with dark green; leaf blades up to 1.3 cm long
and 5 mm wide, mid-vein prominent beneath. In-
florescence 1-flowered, produced from the base of
the leaf axil towards the end of the stem; peduncle
slender, up to 8 mm long. Flowers not fragrant; ovary
muricate, partly obscured by a small floral bract,
about 1 mm long. Sepals and petals similar, incurved,
pale green spotted with dark purple sepals up to 1.1
cm long and 4 mm wide; petals narrower, up to 2.5
mm wide. Lip white, densely spotted with purple,
narrow base, anchor-shaped with two slender lateral
lobes slightly above the middle, incurved. Column

lines.text: short and fleshy with a hairy projecting ligule. (Fig.
34L; Photo. 58).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. The West Indies, Mexi-
co, Belize and Guatemala.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Cayo and Toledo Dis-
tricts. Rare.
HABITAT. On trees in dense moist forest.
FLOWERING SEASON. September.
EtymologY. From the Latin muricatus (rough
with short superficial tubercles) in reference to the
appearance of the ovary.
7. Dichaea panamensis Lindl., Gen. Sp. Orch. Pl.:
208 (1833). Type: Panama, Cuming 1292 (holo. K-
LINDL.!).
Plant epiphytic, small, tufted, often pendant. Stem
slender, compressed,in a cluster and concealed by
the imbricating leaf-sheaths, up to 15 cm long. Lea-
ves distichous, slender, glaucous, about 7 mm apart,
deciduous, up to 3 cm long and 5 mm wide. Inflores-
cence 1-flowered; peduncle slender, from the axil of
the upper leaves, about 1 cm long. Flowers not f
ragrant, greenish-white, with many pinkish-purple
spots, not opening widely, up to 8 mm long. Sepals
and petals similar, up to 8 mm long and 2.5 mm wide.
Lip saggitate, up to 6.5 mm long and 6.5 mm wide at
the base. Column short, fleshy, with a small ligule, up
to 5 mm long. (Fig. 34K; Photo. 59).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Mexico to northern
South America.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Cayo (including the
Mountain Pine Ridge Reserve) and Toledo Districts.
Uncommon.
HABITAT. On trees in dense humid forest.
FLOWERING SEASON. Intermittently throughout
the year. Individual flowers last seven to ten days.
ETyMoLoGY. Named from Panama where the type
specimen was found.
8. Dichaea tuerckheimii Schltr. in Orchis 10: 188
(1916). Type: Guatemala, H. von Türckheim (holo.
Bt).
Dichaea guatemalensis Schltr. in Orchis 10: 190
Plant epiphytic, repent, forming mats of up to 60 cm
across. Stem often branched, elongated, densely
leaved, concealed by leaf-sheaths, up to 1 mm in
diameter. Leaves distichous,
ovate-elliptic, acute, up to 6.5 mm long and 3 mm
wide. Inflorescence from axil of upper leaf; peduncle
about 3 mm apart,
33 Galeottia
filiform, up to 1.5 cm long, 1-flowered; floral bract
suborbicular, up to 2 mm long. Flowers small, pale
green to white, violet spotted. Sepals and petals
similar, spreading, elliptic-lanceolate, acute, up to 6.5
mm long and 2 mm wide. Lip with a fleshy claw, up to
5 mm long; lamina suborbicular-triangular, slightly
concave, up to 3.5 mm wide; callus mammillate.
Column fleshy, up to 2.5 mm long.
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION.
Costa Rica and Panama.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Toledo District. Rare.
HABITAT. Closely appressed to the bark of trees
among mosses in damp forest.
FLOWERING SEASON. August.
EtymoLoGY. Named after German plant collector
H. von Türckheim (1853-1920) who found the type
specimen in Guatemala.
Epiphytic plants, medium-sized with clustered, 2-
leaved pseudobulbs. Leaves plicate. Inflorescences
basal, few-flowered, erect or spreading. Flowers
fleshy, medium-sized to large, often showy. Sepals
and petals free; lateral sepals borne on column-foot;
petals decurrent on column-foot. Lip 3-lobed, with a
fimbriate margin; side lobes small; callus fan-shaped,
grooved. Column incurved, semiterete, fimbriately or
winged at apex, with a prominent foot; pollinia 4,
hard, attached by a quadrate stipe to the viscidium.
There are 11 species, widespread in the American
tropics from Mexico to Peru and Brazil. One is
known from Belize.
The Index Kewensis lists three different genera
called Galeottia: Galeottia Rupr. ex Gal. (1844: Gra-
mineae); Galeottia A. Rich. (1845: Orchidaceae);
and Galeottia Nees in DC. (1847: Acanthaceae). This
listing suggests that Galeottia A. Rich. was a later
homonym and led Hawkes (1963) to propose the
name Mendoncella for this genus. This situation has
recently been reviewed by Christensen (1988 publ.
1989) where he shows that Galeottia Rupr. ex Gal.
(1844) was never validly published and was therefore
nor an earlier homonym. Galeottia A. Rich. becomes
the correct name and Mendoncella Hawkes a
'superfluous substitute name"
EtymoLogY. Named after H. G. Galeotti (1814-
1858), French botanist and the collector of the type
species Galeottia grandiflora A. Rich. & Gal.
Galeottia grandiflora A. Rich. & Gal. in Ann. Sc.
Nat. sér. 3 (3): 25 (1845). Type: Mexico, Galeotti
(holo. BR).

Zygopetalum grandiflorum (A. Rich. & Gal.) Benth.
& Hook. ex Hemsl., Biol. Centr. Am. Bot. 3: 251
Mendoncella grandiflora (A. Rich. & Gal.) A.D.
Hawkes in Orquidea 25: 7 (1963).
Plant epiphytic, large. Pseudobulbs clustered,
elongated pear-shaped, very dark green, covered by
scarious sheaths, up to 10 cm long and 4 cm wide.
Leaves 2 to 3, from the apex of the pseudobulb,
lanceolate, dark green, glossy, with prominent veins,
up to 40 cm long and 8 cm wide. Inflorescence from
the base of the pseudobulb, erect, up to 10-flowered,
up to 26 cm long. Flowers large, showy, not fragrant,
up to 4 cm in diameter. Sepals and petals similar,
yellowish, shading to brownish-red at the margins,
lanceolate, acuminate, recurved at the apex, up to 5
cm long and 1.5 cm wide. Lip hinged to the column-
foot, 3-lobed, concave at the base, margins erose, up
to 1.5 cm wide; lateral lobes brownish-red with
darker veins; mid-lobe cream with dark brownish-red
spots; callus basal, fleshy, ridged and toothed. Col-
umn club- shaped, yellowish-green, up to 3 cm long,
winged at apex. (Fig. 35).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Mexico to Costa Rica.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Cayo District (Moun-
tain Pine Ridge Reserve). Rare.
HABITAT. On trees in damp mountain forest.
FLOWERING SEASON.May and June.
ETymoLoGY. From the Latin grandi (large, big)
and flos (flower) in reference to the large showy
flowers.
Tufted epiphytic herbs, without pseudobulbs. Leaves
many, distichous, arranged in a fan-shape, membra-
naceous to leathery, acute. Inflorescences axillary,
1-flowered. Flowers large, fleshy, showy. Sepals and
petals subsimilar, spreading; lateral sepals and petals
inserted on column-foot. Lip clawed, articulated at
apex of column-foot, basally contracted; callus basal,
long fimbriate. Column arcuate; pollinia 4, flattened,
attached by a short stipe to a flattened viscidium.
There are about ten species from Central America,
South America and Trinidad. One is known from
Belize.
ETymoLogY. Named after the Rev. J.T. Huntley, an
enthusiastic English orchid grower of the early nine-
teenth century.
34. Huntleya Lindl.
35 Koellensteinia
Huntleya fasciata Fowlie in Orch. Digest 30 (9): 281
(1966). Type: Panama, E. Jackson T64 P23 (holo.
UCLA).
Plant epiphytic, up to 30 cm tall. Roots filiform,
glabrous. Leaves erect, 3 to 5, oblanceolate-ligulate,
acuminate, up to 25 cm long and 4 cm wide. Inflores-
from the leaf-axils, 1-flowered, up to 4 cm
cence
long. Flowers showy, glabrous. Sepals and petals
yellowish-green barred with bright red-brown with
yellow tops; sepals elliptic-lanceolate, acuminate, up
to 4 cm long and 1.4 cm wide; lateral sepal slightly
oblique; petals lanceolate-ovate, acuminate, with
recurved tips. Lip deeply blood-stained dark-red;
mid-lobe with narrow yellow border and an acu-
minate yellow tip; up to 5 mm long. Column white,
up to 1.4 cm tall.
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Belize, Panama and
Colombia.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Exact locality not
known. Rare.
HABITAT. On trees in moist forest.
FLOWERING SEASON. Not known.
ETYmoLoGY. From the Latin fasciatus (marked
transversely with broad parallel stripes of colour) in
reference to the colouring of the flower.
NoTE. Reported by Catling & Catling (1988).
35. Koellensteinia Rchb. f.
Terrestrial or epiphytic herbs. Stems short, leafy, of-
ten thickening with age into conspicuous pseudo-
bulbs. Pseudobulbs, if present 1- to 3-leaved at apex,
sometimes with a stalked neck. Leaves linear, petio-
late. Inflorescences lateral, erect or spreading, ra-
cemose. Flowers small to medium-sized. Sepals and
petals similar. Lip articulated to the column-foot,
distinctly 3-lobed; side lobes erect or spreading; mid-
lobe larger, broad. Column very short.
A genus of about ten species. One is known from
Belize.
EtymologY. Named after Captain Kellner von
Koellenstein, an Austrian grower and collector of
plants.

Epiphytic plants withclustered ovoid pseudobulbs
with a single apical leaf, surrounded by papery
sheaths. Leaves plicate, convolute, lanceolate to el-
liptic. Inflorescences 1-flowered, basal, erect or pen-
dent. Flowers medium- sized, resupinate or not.
Dorsal sepal and petals free; lateral sepals connate,
forming a spur-like mentum. Lip 3-lobed, attached to
the apex of the column- foot, with a spur at the base
extending into the mentum; callus low, smooth or
mealy. Column short, fleshy; pollinia 4, hard, waxy,
superposed; viscidium long, wide, lacking a stipe.

Central America to Peru. One is known from Belize.

and orchid grower Henry Teuscher (1891-1984) who
was the curator of the Botanical Garden in Montreal
between 1936 and 1972.

Plant epiphytic, up to 20 cm tall. Pseudobulbs pyri-
form, up to 1.7 cm tall. Leaves 1 or 2, plicate,
lanceolate, acuminate, up to 15 cm long and 3 cm
wide. Inflorescence from the base of the pseudobulb,
1-flowered. Flowers white with violet nerves on the
lateral lobes of the lip. Sepals up to 1.3 cm long and
0.5 cm wide; lateral sepals oblique, adnate to the
column-foot and forming a conspicuous mentum.
Petals 5-nerved, up to 1.3 cm long and 0.4 cm wide.
Lip 3-lobed; midlobe tuberculate, up to 6 mm long
and 4 mm wide; disc with 3 erect, ancipitous, orange-
coloured and verrucose calli in the centre covered
with orange hairs. Column short, semiterete,
glabrous, basally extended into a foot. (Fig. 38).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Mexico, Belize, Hon-
duras, Costa Rica, Colombia and Ecuador.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE.. Exact locality not
known. Rare.
HABITAT. In lowland tropical rain forest.
FLOWERING SEASON. October.
ETymoLoGY. Named after Herrn Hoffgärtner
Pick, who was the gardener at the Berggarten in
Hamburg, and cultivated the type plant there.

the column-foot, simple or 3-lobed, with a distinct
callus. Column basally extended into a prominent
foot; pollinia 4, in 2 pairs on a transverse scale-like

lines.text: SUBTRIBE MAXILLARIINAE BENTH.
Plants epiphytic, lithophytic or rarely terrestrial,
tufted or rhizomatous. Rhizome short to elongate,
creeping, enclosed by papery sheaths. Pseudobulbs
clustered or remote on rhizome. Leaves distichous.
Inflorescences 1-flowered, fasciculate, glomerate or
solitary, axillary from basal sheaths. Flower small to
large and showy. Sepals and petals similar; lateral
sepals adnate to the column-foot forming a mentum.
Lip adnate to, or articulate with, the column-foot,
sometimes forming a saccate nectary; disc usually
with a fleshy callus. Column stout, extended at base
to form a distinct foot; pollinia 4, waxy; viscidium
semilunate.
Maxillaria is one of the largest genera of American
orchids with about 300 species. Twenty are known
from Belize.
Some species produce a waxy substance on the
callus that is collected by bees and used in
construction (Porsch, 1909).
ETYMoLoGY. From the Latin maxilla (jaw-bone)
alluding to the appearance of the column and lip of
some species which resemble the jaws of an insect.

Sched. Orch. 8: 57 (1925). Type: Costa Rica, Peralta,

Plant epiphytic, small, up to 13 cm tall. Roots numer-
ous, fibrous, branched. Pseudobulbs up to 1.6 cm
long, monophyllous, concealed by a pair of imbricat-
ing distichous leaf-bearing sheaths. Leaves elliptic-
oblong, petioled, up to 10 cm long and 2.2 cm wide;
petiole laterally flattened, up to 2.2 cm long. Inflores-
cence shorter than the leaves, 1-flowered; peduncle
filiform, up to 4.5 cm long. Flowers large, erect,
white, lateral lobes of lip with red-violet nerves on
the upper half. Lateral sepals triangular-lanceolate,
up to 2 cm long and 7.2 mm wide, many-nerved,
forming a mentum with the column-foot; dorsal sepal
up to 2 cm long and 4.9 mm wide. Petals lanceolate,
up to 1.8 cm long and 3.7 mm wide. Lip small, erect,
3-lobed at apex, up to 1.2 cm long and 6 mm wide,
sides upcurving; callus lingulate. Column extended
into a long foot, short, stout, up to 4 mm long.
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Belize, Nicaragua,
Costa Rica and Panama.

cm long and 0.4 cm wide. Lip 3-lobed about the

short, bluntly triangular and clasping the column;

to 1.5 cm long. (Fig. 46M; Photo 68).

18. Maxillaria tenuifolia Lindl. in Bot. Reg. 23: sub.

Maxillaria augustifolia Hook., Ic. Pl. 4: t. 348
Plant epiphytic, a cluster of prostrate scaly rhizomes.
Pseudobulbs ovoid, 3 cm apart on the rhizome, dark
green, up to 4 cm long and 1.5 cm wide, unifoliate,
subtended by several sheaths. Leaves linear, grass-
green, up to 20 cm long and 1 cm wide. Inflorescence
1-flowered, subtended by several sheaths, from the
bases of the pseudobulbs. Flowers not fragrant, very
variable in both size and colour; pedicellate ovary up
to 3 cm long. Sepals and petals lemon- to golden-
yellow; petals often tinged with reddish-brown on the
outside, curl back at the tips, up to 1.4 cm long and
0.4 cm wide; sepals up to 1.7 cm long and 0.6 cm
wide; lateral sepals forming a mentum with the
column-foot. Lip deep reddish-brown tipped with
yellow, fleshy, erect, fleshy, obscurely 3-lobed in the
middle, rounded to truncate at apex, up to 1.3 cm long
and 0.6 cm wide; disc with a triangular-subquadrate
glossy callus. Column semiterete, arcuate, up to 1 cm
long. (Fig. 47; Photo. 81).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Mexico to Panama.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Belize, Cayo (including
the Mountain Pine Ridge Reserve) Stann Creek and
Toledo Districts. Common.
HABITAT. On trees in moist forest.
FLOWERING SEASON. July to March. Flowers last
about a week.
40 Mormolyca
ETyMoLoGY. From the Latin variabilis (variable)
in reference to the variable size and colour of the
flowers.
NoTE. M. variabilis is known, in some parts of
Guatemala, as "La Gloria'.
Epiphytic herbs. Rhizome rather short. Pseudobulbs
1- to 4-leaved. Leaves leathery. Inflorescences from
the base of the pseudobulb or the axils of bracts on the
rhizome, 1-flowered; peduncles elongate, slender.
Sepals free. Petals and lip smaller than the sepals. Lip
hinged to the base of the column, simple or 3-lobed,
with a median callus. Column without a foot; pollinia
4, waxy; viscidium lunate.
A genus of six species distributed from Mexico to
Brazil and Peru. One is known from Belize.
The genus is closely allied to Maxillaria but sepa-
rated on the basis of the flowers lacking a column-
foot and mentum.
ETymoLoGY. From the Greek mormolyca (hob-
goblin) alluding to the supposedly grotesque appear-
ance and colouration of the flower.
Mormolyca ringens (Lindl.) Schltr. in Orchideen:
436 (1914). Type: Mexico, Schiede (holo. K!).
Trigonidium ringens Lindl. in Bot. Reg. 26: Misc. 57
Mormolyca lineolata Fenzl in Denkschr. Akad. Wiss.
Plant epiphytic, erect spreading, up to 30 cm tall.
Pseudobulbs clustered, or up to 3 cm apart, ovoid to
ellipsoid, flattened, finely wrinkled, up to 5 cm long
and 3 cm wide, unifoliate, subtended by prominent
sheaths when young; sheaths brown, papery. Leaves
linear-elliptic, up to 35 cm long and 3.5 cm wide.
Inflorescence few, more or less erect, produced in
succession; peduncle wiry, persistent, up to 28 cm
long, provided with several papery sheaths. Flowers
greenish-yellow, purple-veined; pedicellate ovaries
slender, up to 4.5 cm long. Sepals up to 1.8 cm long;
dorsal sepal concave, keeled at the apex, up to 8 mm
wide; lateral sepals directed downwards, curved to-
wards each other, convex up to 7 mm wide. Petals
directed upwards beneath the dorsal sepal, curved
towards each other and overlapping at the tips, with
strongly recurved margins, up to 1.4 cm long and 5
mm wide. Lip 3-lobed below the middle, up to 9 mm
long and 5 mm wide; lateral lobes small, triangular;
mid-lobe strongly decurved, suffused with maroon,

Plant usually epiphytic, erect to spreading, up to 50
cm tall. Pseudobulbs bifoliate, up to 9 cm long and
3.5 cm wide, subtended by fibrous sheaths. Leaves
linear-oblanceolate, up to 45 cm long and 2.5 cm

subtending the pseudobulbs, 1-flowered; peduncle

veins, the lip green marked with purple. Sepals
oblong-elliptic, up to 4.2 cm long and 2 cm wide.

and 0.7 cm wide. Lip 3-lobed, up to 1 cm long and 0.6
cm wide; side-lobes thin; mid-lobe fleshy, verrucose,
decurved-reflexed; disc with a linear callus. Column
short, stout, straight, up to 0.7 cm long. (Fig. 49;
Photo. 83).

DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Found in all districts,
often persisting on isolated trees after land clea-
rance. Very common.

Mouth' orchid. Plants tend to form large clumps and,

42 Coryanthes
SUBTRIBE STANHOPEINAE BENTH.
42. Coryanthes Hook.
Large epiphytic herbs. Pseudobulbs clustered, rigid,
2-leaved. Leaves plicate, prominently veined, petio-
late. Inflorescences from the base of the pseudobulb,
commonly
hanging,
elongate. Flowers in a loose raceme, large, showy
and scented. Sepals spreading or reflexed; dorsal
sepal smaller than the laterals. Petals smaller than the
sepals, twisted. Lip pendent, complexly 3-lobed,
fleshy; hypochile formed from side lobes, cup-
shaped; mesochile elongate, sometimes fluted; epi-
chile large, galeate. Column large, with a reflexed
apex, provided at the base with 2 wing- or horn-like
glands; pollinia 2, waxy.
There are about 15 species, all in Central America.
One is known from Belize.
Commonly known as 'Bucket Orchids'. They are
almost always found on the nests of certain tree-
dwelling ants and can be difficult to cultivate in the
absence of such ants.
The flowers of this genus are among the most
complex in the orchid family and are remarkably
adapted to insect pollination. Their powerful scent
attracts male perfume-collecting bees and sooner or
later one falls, or is pushed, into the bucket-like
epichile of the lip. This is partly filled with a sugary
fluid that is secreted by the glands at the base of the
column. With its wings wet and the sides of the
bucket slippery, the bee's only escape is through a
tunnel formed by the apex of the epichile and the
reflexed tip of the column. As it squeezes through the
gap the pollinia become attached to its back and
pollination is effected if it repeats the procedure in
another flower.
EtymoLoGY. From the Greek korys (helmet) and
anthos (flower) referring to the characteristically
shaped epichile of the lip.

from Toledo district as C. maculata Hook. While

43. Gongora Ruiz & Pav.
Throughout the year.
43 Gongora
was
from the base of the pseudobulb, hanging, few- to
many-flowered. Flowers in a raceme, rather large,
fragrant. Dorsal sepal more or less joined to the sides
of the column. Lateral sepals joined to the column-
foot. Petals joined to the sides of the column, much
smaller then the sepals. Lip joined or hinged to the
column-foot, complexly 3-lobed, fleshy, often pro-
vided with horns or bristle-like projections. Column
slender, curved, basally extended into a foot; pollinia
2, ovoid to narrowly oblong.
A genus of about 25 species, all in the American
tropics. Four are known from Belize.
Gongora species are pollinated by Euglossine bees
by means of the fall-through mechanism. The bee
enters between the lip and column turning upside
down. The bee crawls along the underside of the lip,
scratching the cavity of the hypochile. Occasionally
they drop and while falling they rotate and slide down
the inside surface of the column picking up the polli-
narium under their dorsal abdomen (van de Pijl &
Dodson, 1966).
The genus Gongora has been reviewed and revised
in a series of articles by R. Jenny (1979-1991, 1985).
EtymoLogY. Named after Don Antonio Cabal-
lero y Gongora, one time Viceroy of New Granada
(Columbia and Equador) and later Bishop of Cordo-
ba, Spain.

most confusing and has been reviewed by Whitten

flowers and Ruiz & Pavon's description and illustra-
tion is rather vague. This has meant that many reports
of G. quinquenervis have been inaccurate.

Plant epiphytic, erect-spreading, up to 40 cm tall.

tened, strongly ridged, rather glossy, 2-leaved, up to 8

45 Stanhopea
Epiphytic herbs, sometimes lithophytic or terrestrial.
Pseudobulbs clustered, ridged, unifoliate. Leaves
large, plicate, prominently veined, petiolate; petiole
slender and grooved. Inflorescences from the base of
the pseudobulb, hanging, 1- to several-flowered;
bracts large. Flowers in a loose raceme, large, showy,
strongly scented. Sepals and petals spreading to
reflexed; petals smaller than the sepals. Lip joined to
the base of the column, complex, fleshy, often pro-
vided with horns. Column elongate, often winged;
pollinia 2, waxy.
There are about 25 species, all in the American
tropics. Four are known from Belize.
These are frequently cultivated plants and are pol-
linated by male perfume-collecting bees (L. van der
Pijl & Dodson, 1966). The large bizarre flowers are
very striking but, unfortunately, short-lived.

GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Mexico to Columbia

or in moist to wet broad-leaved forest between 400
and 750m.

last about four days.
EtymoLoGY. From the Latin oculatus (eyed, with
an eye) in reference to the two large maroon 'eyes' on

SUBTRIBE ORNITHOCEPHALINAE SCHLTR.
Epiphytic plants without pseudobulbs. Stems short,
completely covered with distichous, imbricating
leaf-sheaths. Leaves fleshy, equitant, arranged in a
fan-shape. Inflorescences axillary, racemose, few- to
several-flowered. Flowers small. Sepals and petals
similar, free. Lip entire or lobed; callus basally thick-
ened, inflexed in front. Column short, without wings
or a foot; anther beaked; pollinia 4, waxy.
A genus of about 50 species distributed throughout
the American tropics. Two are known from Belize.
EtymoLogY. From the Greek ornithos (bird) and
kephale (head) alluding to the curious shape of the
column-apex, which resembles a bird's head.

flowers greenish-white to greenish-yellow

Plant epiphytic, small and fan-shaped, without pseu-
dobulbs, normally pendent. Leaves somewhat fleshy,
equitant, up to eighteen in number, linear, acute, up to
10 cm long and 6 mm wide; sheaths imbricated, up to
1.5 cm long. Inflorescence 1 or more per plant, ra-
cemose, many-flowered, from the axil of the leaf-
sheath, up to 11 cm long. Flowers not fragrant, small,
white with a greenish lip; pedicellate ovaries
glabrous, up to 5 mm long. Sepals spreading, subor-
bicular, dorsally carinate, glabrous, up to 2.3 mm
long and 1.8 mm wide. Petals cuneate-flabellate, up
to 3.5 mm long and 4.2 mm wide. Lip deeply 3-
lobed, base triangular-cordate, up to 5 mm in diame-
ter. Column short, fleshy, up to 3 mm long; rostellum
produced into a long beak. Capsule broadly 6-
winged. (Fig. 55; Photo. 94).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Mexico to Costa Rica,
and Trinidad.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Orange Walk, Cayo (in-
cluding the Mountain Pine Ridge Reserve), Stann
Creek and Toledo Districts. Fairly common.
HABITAT. On trees in moist forest, usually low
down on trunks in well shaded situations.
FLOWERING SEASON. March to May.
EtymoLogY. From the Latin gladiatus (sword-
like) in reference to the shape of the leaves.
47 Brassia
SUBTRIBE ONCIDIINAE BENTH.
Epiphytic, occasionally lithophytic or terrestrial
herbs. Rhizome stout, creeping. Pseudobulbs ovoid to
cylindrical, 1- to 3-leaved. Leaves linear or elliptic-
oblong, leathery. Inflorescences from the base of a
pseudobulb, few- to many-flowered. Flowers in a
raceme, often showy. Sepals spreading, free, long and
narrow. Petals similar to the sepals but shorter. Lip
simple, with a basal callus. Column short, stout,
wingless; pollinia 2, obovoid.
A genus of about 20 species, widely distributed in
the American tropics. Two are known from Belize.
This genus is frequently cultivated and often
known as 'spider orchids' on account of their long
slender sepals. The resemblance of the flowers to
spiders is probably not accidental since spider-
hunting wasps have been observed to attack them
and, in the process, effect pollination. Dodson (1990)
has observed female wasps of the genera Pepsis and
Campsomeris pollinating species of Brassia. These
wasps hunt spiders and paralyse them by stinging,
then carry them to their nests and lay their eggs on
them. The larva of the wasps consume the fresh, but
paralysed, tissues of the spider. Pollination is effected
by an attempt to 'capture' the column and in the
unsuccessful attempt to drag away their 'prey' the
pollinia are placed on the head of the wasp.
Brassia is allied to Oncidium with which some
species have been crossed to give rise to the hybrid
genus x Brassidium.
ETyMoLoGY. Named after William Brass (died
1783), the English plant collector, botanical artist and
gardener to the 1st Duke of Northumberland.

lines.text: 50. Leochilus Knowles & Westcott
Plants small, tufted, epiphytic herbs with pseudobul-
bous stems. Pseudobulbs covered by 1 to several
leaf-sheaths at base and 1- to 2-leaved above. Leaves
leathery, lanceolate. Inflorescences racemose or pani-
culate, laxly few- flowered. Flowers small, inconspi-
cuous. Sepals and petals spreading, free or connate.
Lip adnate to base of column, entire or 3-lobed; callus
fleshy. Column lacking a foot, bearing stelidia on
each side near middle, truncate at apex; rostellum
elongate; pollinia 2, waxy.
A genus of about 15 species distributed from the
West Indies and Mexico to Argentina. One is known
from Belize.
Leochilus is allied to Oncidium but differs in that
the anther is produced in front into a membranceous
appendage equalling or mostly longer than the locule
(Bechtel et al., 1992).
ETyMoLogY. From the Greek leios (smooth) and
cheilos (lip) referring to the smooth surface of the
lip.
Leochilus labiatus (Sw.) Kuntze in Rev. Gen. Pl.: 656
(1891). Type: Jamaica, Swartz (holo. UPS).
Epidendrum labiatum Sw., Prodr: 124 (1788).
Rodriguezia cochlearis Lindl. in Ann. Nat. Hist. 5:
Leochilus gracilis Schltr. in Fedde, Repert. Sp. Nov.
Plant epiphytic, small, erect, up to 25 cm tall; the
entire plant often tinged with red. Pseudobulbs
clustered, ovoid, unifoliate, up to 20 mm long and 12
mm wide, subtended by scarious leaf-sheaths. Leaves
from apex of pseudobulb, broadly elliptic, up to 7 cm
long and 2 cm wide. Inflorescence from base of
pseudobulb, racemose, few-flowered; peduncle with
lanceolate bracts of up to 9 mm long. Flowers small,
translucent, yellow or pale green, suffused with red-
brown; pedicellate ovary up to 10 mm long. Dorsal
sepal ovate-elliptic, arcuate over the column, up to
6.5 mm long and 3 mm wide; lateral sepals deflexed,
50 Leochilus
united to the middle, up to 6.5 mm long and 1.5 mm
wide above the point of union. Petals projected fore-
wards, elliptic-oblong, up to 6 mm long and 2.8 mm
wide. Lip strongly arcuate, spreading above, base
appressed against column, up to 8 mm long and 4.5
mm wide; disc fleshly-thickened. Column thick, up to
3 mm long, with a denticulate membrane at apex and
a slender linear arm on each side about the middle.
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. The West Indies, Belize
to Panama.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Stann Creek District.
Uncommon.
HABITAT. On trees in moist valley regions or open
mountain forest.
FLOWERING SEASON. March to June.
ETymoLoGY. From the Latin labiatus (lipped, lip-
shaped).
NoTE. Reported by Catling & Catling (1988).
Epiphytic herbs. Rhizome short, creeping. Pseudo-
bulbs slender, clustered, unifoliate. Leaves linear-
lanceolate, leathery or fleshy. Inflorescences from the
base of the pseudobulb, few- to many-flowered.
Flowers in a raceme. Sepals and petals similar, lan-
ceolate, spreading, free. Lip joined to the base of the
column, simple or 3-lobed, concave, with a basal
callus. Column erect, apex with an oblong hood over
the anther; pollinia 2, pyriform; stipe linear-oblong;
viscidium small.
A genus of about five species, all in the American
tropics. One is known from Belize.
Leucohyle has been included within Trichopilia by
some recent authors but is distinguished by its more
slender growth, the smaller flowers and the lateral
lobes of the lip, which do not form a tube enclosing
the column.
EtymoLogY. From the Greek leucos (white) and
hyle (wood or stuff) probably referring to the white
indumentum on the floral axis.

Epiphytic tufted herbs, lacking pseudobulbs. Stems
clustered, slender, flattened, leafy, concealed by the
leaves. Leaves usually numerous, distichous, later-
ally flattened. Inflorescences from theupper leaf
axils, commonly short; floral bracts amplexicaul, of-
ten conspicuous. Flowers white or yellow often
marked with red or chestnut-brown. Sepals and petals
similar, free,spreading or reflexed. Lipsimpleor
3-lobed, with a basal callus. Column short, 2-winged;
pollinia 2, waxy.
A genus of about 30 species, all in the American
tropics. Two are known from Belize. A third species,
L oerstedii Rchb. f., was reported by Siegerist (1984)
but, according to Catling & Catling (1988), the speci-
men that was the basis for this report is referable to L.
pittieri.
Lockhartia are sometimes known as 'braided
orchids'. The flowers of many species of Lockhartia
resemble those of Oncidium, but the very different
inflorescences and gereral form of the plant suggest
that the relationship is rather a remote one.
EtymoLoGY. Named after David Lockhart (1818-
1846), the first Superintendent of the Trinidad Bota-
nic Gardens and collector of the type species, L.
elegans.

Small to large epiphytic, lithophytic or terrestrial
plants with short to long rhizomes. Pseudobulbs
small to large, 1- to 2-leaved at apex, subtended by
sheaths. Leaves flat to terete, membranaceous to

often with a yellow lip, inconspicuous to showy.

pollinia 2, waxy, deeply sulcate.
55. Oncidium Sw.
55 Oncidium
A large genus of over 400 species native to the
American tropics and subtropics. Eight are known
from Belize.
Many species of Oncidium are pollinated by an-
throphorid bees of the genus Centris, many of which
gather oil from the flower instead of, or as well as,
pollen. These bees display strong territorial behav-
iour. Male bees set up territories and drive away other
flying insects which invade their territory. When the
flowers of an Oncidium, which resemble insects,
move, the bees attack them, striking the flowers with
their heads. The viscidium attaches to the front of the
bee, between the compound eyes, and the stipe
depresses holding the pollinia in front of the bee. This
pollination mechanism is called pseudoantagonism
(van de Pijl & Dodson, 1966).
EtymologY. From the Greek onkos (a pad or
mass) referring to the fleshy warty callus on the lip of
many species.

ridge, white spotted with red-brown. Column short,

the apex, up to 5 mm long. (Photo. 110).

5. Oncidium ensatum Lindl. in Bot. Reg. 28: Misc.
17 (1842). Type: Guatemala, cult. Loddiges (holo. K,
not located).
Plant terrestrial, usually tall and graceful. Pseudo-
bulbs in a small clump, flattened, up to 10 cm long
and 4 cm wide, bifoliate, subtended by broad over-
lapping sheaths. Leaves erect, linear-ensiform, up to
90 cm long and 3.5 cm wide, yellow-green, keeled.
Inflorescence from the base of the pseudobulb, en-
closed in sheathing bracts, paniculate, up to 2.5 m tall
with numerous widely spaced branches. Flowers
slightly fragrant, numerous, small, up to 2.8 cm long
and 2.2 cm wide. Sepals and petals similar,
chocolate-brown, tipped and edged with greenish-
yellow and with occasional yellow spotting,
somewhat reflexed with an undulate margin, up to 1.6
cm long and 7 mm wide. Lip bright yellow, side lobes
with a brown base, broadly violin-shaped, 3-lobed,
up to 1.8 cm long and 1.3 cm wide, mid-lobe sepa-
rated from side lobes by a broad isthmus; callus at the
base of the lip, tuberculate, fleshy. Column short,
fleshy, up to 5 mm long. (Photo. 111).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Mexico to Honduras.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Belize, Cayo (including
the Mountain Pine Ridge Reserve) and Toledo Dis-
tricts. Fairly common.

Plant epiphytic, tall. Pseudobulbs small, often
covered with scarious sheaths, unifoliate. Leaves
thickened, ridgid, leathery, dark green and in-
distinctly spotted and blotched with purple, up to 30
cm long and 7 cm wide. Inflorescence arising from
the base of the pseudobulb, up to 110 cm long,
paniculate with one or more small branches, each
with several flowers; peduncle slender and wiry.
Flowers not fragrant, up to 2 cm in diameter. Sepals
and petals similar, brown with a greenish-white patch
at the base or spotted with brown on pale green. Lip
with a golden yellow base, side lobes glossy, very
dark magenta appearing almost black. Column short,
winged, up to 5 mm long. (Photo. 112)
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Mexico to Honduras.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Cayo District. Rare.
HABITAT. On isolated trees and in riverine forest.
FLOWERING SEASON. March to June. Flowers last
three to five weeks.
ETYMOLOGY. Named after Jean Linden (1817-
1898), a Luxemburg born botanical explorer, orchid
collector, nurseryman at Ghent and founder of the
Horticulture Internationale in Brussels, who found
the type specimen.
7. Oncidium sphacelatum Lindl., Sert. Orch.:
sub.t.48 (1841). Type: Mexico, Hartweg (holo. K-
LINDL.! but specimen lacking provenance).
Plant epiphytic, in large clumps, often extremely
large masses. Pseudobulbs flattened, somewhat
ridged, up to 20 cm long and 5 cm wide, bearing
either one, or more usually two, leaves. Leaves rigid,
erect, up to 70 cm long and 5 cm wide, light green.
Inflorescence from the base of the pseudobulb, pani-
culate, much branched and many-flowered, up to

fleshy, deeply channelled, up to 30 cm long and 1.1
cm wide, tapering to a sharp point, dark green with
purple spots. Inflorescence from base of pseudobulb,
more or less erect, racemose, up to 16-flowered.
Flowers not fragrant, clustered, small, on the upper
third of the inflorescence, up to 2.5 cm long and 2 cm
wide. Sepals and petals similar, curved forewards at
the tip, greenish-yellow blotched with red-brown,
margins yellow and undulate; sepals up to 1.4 cm
long and 0.8 cm wide, spathulate; petals up to 1.3 cm
long and 0.6 cm wide, oblong. Lip 3-lobed, with the
mid-lobe the largest, yellow spotted with red-brown,
up to 2 cm long and 2.5 cm wide; callus between the
side lobes, walnut-like with a prominent central
ridge, white spotted with red-brown. Column short,
stout, whitish with purple spots, two small wings at
the apex, up to 5 mm long. (Photo. 110).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. The West Indies, Mexi-
co to Paraguay.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Cayo District (Moun-
tain Pine Ridge Reserve). Very rare.
HABITAT. On trees in wet riverine forest.
FLOWERING SEASON. February. Flowers last about
three weeks.
EtymoLogY. Derivation not known.
5. Oncidium ensatum Lindl. in Bot. Reg. 28: Misc.
17 (1842). Type: Guatemala, cult. Loddiges (holo. K,
not located).
Plant terrestrial, usually tall and graceful. Pseudo-
bulbs in a small clump, flattened, up to 10 cm long
and 4 cm wide, bifoliate, subtended by broad over-
lapping sheaths. Leaves erect, linear-ensiform, up to
90 cm long and 3.5 cm wide, yellow-green, keeled.
Inflorescence from the base of the pseudobulb, en-
closed in sheathing bracts, paniculate, up to 2.5 m tall
with numerous widely spaced branches. Flowers
slightly fragrant, numerous, small, up to 2.8 cm long
and 2.2 cm wide. Sepals and petals similar,
chocolate-brown, tipped and edged with greenish-
yellow and with occasional yellow spotting,
somewhat reflexed with an undulate margin, up to 1.6
cm long and 7 mm wide. Lip bright yellow, side lobes
with a brown base, broadly violin-shaped, 3-lobed,
up to 1.8 cm long and 1.3 cm wide, mid-lobe sepa-
rated from side lobes by a broad isthmus; callus at the
base of the lip, tuberculate, fleshy. Column short,
fleshy, up to 5 mm long. (Photo. 111).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Mexico to Honduras.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Belize, Cayo (including
the Mountain Pine Ridge Reserve) and Toledo Dis-
tricts. Fairly common.
55 Oncidium
HABITAT. In open grassy areas (savanna), moun-
tain and coastal pine ridge areas, often in dense grass
associated with small bushes.
FLOWERING SEASON. December to May. Flowers
last two to three weeks.
EtymoLogY. From the Latin ensatus (sword-
shaped) in reference to the sword-shaped leaves.
NoTE. This species is unique among Belizean
Oncidiums in its obligate terrestrial habitat.
6. Oncidium lindenii Brongn. in Lem., Hort. Univ.
3: 372 (1842). Type: Mexico, Campeche, Linden s.n.
(holo. BR).
O. lindenii Lodd. ex Lindl., Sert. Orch.: sub.t.48,
n.101 (1841) nom. illeg.
Plant epiphytic, tall. Pseudobulbs small, often
covered with scarious sheaths, unifoliate. Leaves
thickened, ridgid, leathery, dark green and in-
distinctly spotted and blotched with purple, up to 30
cm long and 7 cm wide. Inflorescence arising from
the base of the pseudobulb, up to 110 cm long,
paniculate with one or more small branches, each
with several flowers; peduncle slender and wiry.
Flowers not fragrant, up to 2 cm in diameter. Sepals
and petals similar, brown with a greenish-white patch
at the base or spotted with brown on pale green. Lip
with a golden yellow base, side lobes glossy, very
dark magenta appearing almost black. Column short,
winged, up to 5 mm long. (Photo. 112)
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Mexico to Honduras.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Cayo District. Rare.
HABITAT. On isolated trees and in riverine forest.
FLOWERING SEASON. March to June. Flowers last
three to five weeks.
ETYMOLOGY. Named after Jean Linden (1817-
1898), a Luxemburg born botanical explorer, orchid
collector, nurseryman at Ghent and founder of the
Horticulture Internationale in Brussels, who found
the type specimen.
7. Oncidium sphacelatum Lindl., Sert. Orch.:
sub.t.48 (1841). Type: Mexico, Hartweg (holo. K-
LINDL.! but specimen lacking provenance).
Plant epiphytic, in large clumps, often extremely
large masses. Pseudobulbs flattened, somewhat
ridged, up to 20 cm long and 5 cm wide, bearing
either one, or more usually two, leaves. Leaves rigid,
erect, up to 70 cm long and 5 cm wide, light green.
Inflorescence from the base of the pseudobulb, pani-
culate, much branched and many-flowered, up to

diameter, showy. Sepals and petals similar, golden-

two thirds, reflexed at the top, undulate margins, up to

Column with small wings, fleshy, up to 6 mm long.
(Fig. 66; Photo. 113).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Mexico to El Salvador.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. All districts. Common.
HABITAT. On trees in forest and thicket.
FLOWERING SEASON. December to May. Flowers
last two to three weeks.
ETymoLoGY. From the Latin sphacelatus (with
brown or blackish speckling) in reference to the
colouring of the sepals and petals.
8. Oncidium stipitatum Lindl. in Benth., Bot. Voy.
Sulph.: 172 (1846). Type: Panama, G.W. Barclay 958
(holo. BM!).
Plant epiphytic, tufted, often pendent. Pseudobulbs
small, usually unifoliate, up to 2 cm long and 1 cm
wide. Leaf long-linear, arcuate, semiterete, a single
groove runs down the centre of the leaf ending in a
sharp point, up to 70 cm long and 1.5 cm wide.
Inflorescence from the base of the pseudobulb, pani-
culate, up to 100 cm long. Flowers showy, numerous,
up to 2 cm in diameter and 1.8 cm wide; lip bright
yellow, sepals and petals yellow streaked with red,
column yellow with red markings. Sepals spreading,
reflexed, lanceolate; dorsal sepal hooded; lateral
sepals up to 0.8 cm long and 0.4 cm wide. Petals
spreading, lanceolate, up to 1 cm long and 0.5 cm
wide, undulate margins. Lip deeply 3-lobed, up to 1.8
cm long and 1.5 cm wide; lateral lobes linear-
lanceolate, acuminate, wing-like; mid-lobe larger
than lateral lobes, semiorbicular, margins undulate;
callus red-brown. Column winged, up to 1 cm long
and 0.3 cm wide; wings up to 0.4 cm wide.
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Belize and Panama.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Cayo District (Moun-
tain Pine Ridge Reserve). Uncommon.
HABITAT. On trees in open mountain forest at
about 650 m.
FLOWERING SEASON. Not known.
ETymoLoGY. From the Latin stipitatus (provided
with a stalk).
NOTES. O. stipitatum was reported by Siegerist
(1984) on the basis of a specimen from Belize at EAP.
We have not seen this specimen and have not been
56 Psygmorchis
able to find any other reports from Belize. There are
no herbarium specimens of this plant at Kew and the
description has been taken from a drawing in the Kew
herbarium (Jones & Scully 644.62, Feb. 28, 1963/
487). The plant is very similar to O. ascendens and
differs in a number of minor characteristics. We have
not included it in the key.
56. Psygmorchis Dodson & Dressler
Dwarf epiphytes lacking pseudobulbs. Stem very
short. Leaves distichous in a fan, equitant, succulent.
Inflorescences lateral, 1-flowered. Flowers large for
plant, with a large yellow lip. Dorsal sepal and petals
free; lateral sepals partially united. Lip large, 4-lobed,
at right angles to column; callus basal. Column
winged, short; pollinia 2, hard, laterally attached to to
a long narrow stipe; viscidium 1.
A genus of about five species distributed in Central
and South America. One is known from Belize.
The genus Psygmorchis is a segregate of Oncidium
established by C. Dodson & R. Dressler in 1972. The
plants lack pseudobulbs, have iridiform leaves and
condensed inflorescences producing one flower at a
time.
EtymoLogY. From the Greek psygma (fan) and
orchis (an orchid) in reference to the characteristic
growth habit of the plant.
Psygmorchis pusilla (L) Dodson & Dressler in Phy-
tologia 24: 288 (1972). Type: Surinam, C. Dahlberg
(holo. S).
Epidendrum pusillum L., Sp. Pl., Ed.2, 2: 1352
Oncidium pusillum (L.) Rchb. f. in Walp. Ann. Bot.
O. iridifolium Kunth, Nov. Gen. Sp. Pl. 1: 344
Plant epiphytic, small, fan-shaped, occuring singly or
in a cluster, pendent, without pseudobulbs. Leaves
flattened, from a short rhizome, fleshy, sword-
shaped, up to 7 cm long and 1.5 cm wide. Inflores-
cence from the axils of the leaves, 1-flowered, usual-
ly with several bracts at the apex of the peduncle.
Flowers large and showy in relation to the size of the
plant, not fragrant, yellow with reddish spots on the
large lip and petals, up to 2.5 cm long and 2 cm wide;
pedicellate ovary up to 7 mm long. Sepals and petals
similar. Lip much larger than the sepals and petals,
3-lobed at the base; callus fleshy. Column short, thick,
up to 4 mm long. (Fig. 67; Photo. 114).

lines.text: GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. The West Indies, Mexi-
co to northern South America.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Cayo, Stann Creek and
Toledo Districts. Uncommon.
HABITAT. On trees and notably in citrus planta-
tions.
FLOWERING SEASON. Intermittent throughout the
year. Flowers last several weeks.
EtymoLoGY. From the Latin pusillus (very small,
insignificant) in reference to the very small plant
S1Ze.
NOTES. This species has proved difficult to grow
in cultivation. The seed pods are large, up to 2.5 cm
long and 1.8 cm wide, and prominently 6-winged.
Epiphytic herbs. Rhizome short. Pseudobulbs
clustered, unifoliate. Leaves leathery. Inflorescences
from the base of the pseudobulb, 1- to few-flowered.
Flowers large and showy. Sepals and petals similar,
spreading, narrow, twisted or contorted. Lip joined to
the base of the column, more or less 3-lobed, with or
without a callus; lateral lobes forming a tube enclos-
ing the column. Column slender, clavate, erect, 2-
winged; pollinia 2, waxy; stipe broadly triangular.
A genus of about 25 species, all native to the
tropics of Central and South America. One is known
from Belize.
ETYMOLoGY. From the Greek trichos (hair) and
pilos (felt, felt-cap) referring to the fact that the anther
is concealed below a cap surmounted with three tufts
of hair.
Trichopilia tortilis Lindl., Introd. Nat. Syst. Bot.
ed.2: 446 (1836). Type: Mexico, G. Barker (holo.
K-LINDL.! but specimen lacking provenance).
Plant epiphytic, erect-spreading, up to 28 cm tall.
Pseudobulbs more or less oblong, strongly flattened,
up to 9 cm long and 2 cm wide, more or less enclosed
in sheaths when young; sheaths papery, brown-
spotted. Leaves narrowly elliptic, dark green, acute,
57. Trichopilia Lindl.
57 Trichopilia
folded at the base, up to 24 cm long and 4.6 cm wide.
Inflorescence 1- to 2-flowered; peduncle up to 8 cm
long, enclosed at base in several sheaths. Flowers
faintly fragrant; pedicellate ovaries up to 6 cm long.
Sepals and petals brownish-purple bordered with
pale green, twisted, up to 6 cm long and 1 cm wide.
Lip broadly obovate in outline, white spotted with
pink, yellow within the tubular portion, up to 5 cm
long and 4 cm wide across the lateral lobes when
spread; mid-lobe spreading, somewhat decurved,
notched at the apex, with undulate margins. Column
green at base, white above, up to 2 cm long. (Fig. 68;
Photo. 115).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Mexico to Nicaragua.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Toledo District. Rare.
HABITAT. On trees in wet broad-leaved forest at
about 750 m.
FLOWERING SEASON. October to January. Flowers
last about two weeks.
ETyMoLoGY. From the Latin tortilis (twisted) in
reference to the twisted appearance of the sepals and
petals.
NotEs. The large and colourful flowers with their
strangely twisted sepals and petals are most attrac-
tive.
SUBTRIBE BLETIINAE BENTH.
Terrestrial or, rarely, epiphytic herbs. Pseudobulbs
corm-like. Leaves few, from the apex of the corm,
plicate, petiolate. Inflorescences from the side of the
corm. Flowers often showy. Sepals and petals simi-
lar, free, spreading. Lip joined to the column-foot,
simple or three-lobed, variously crested. Column
curved, more or less winged above, basally extended
into a short foot; pollinia 8, in 2 sets of 4, hard,
compressed.
A genus of about 30 closely allied species, all in
the American tropics and subtropics and with the
largest number in Mexico. One is known from Bel-
ize.

Schweinf. as occuring in Belize from a collection by
Gentle (9736) on Colonel English Pine Ridge, Cayo
District. Catling & Catling (1988) have examined the
specimen in the Lundell Herbarium and found it to be

and petals similar, more or less spreading. Lip tubular
below, spreading above, enclosing the column, often
provided with calli near the base. Column 3-lobed at
the apex; pollinia 8, granulose.

resemble those of Cattleya but commonly fade with-
in a few hours of opening. Many species exhibit
gregarious flowering, nearly all plants at any one
locality flowering on the same morning. Sobralia
plants havesuccessfully adapted themselves to
growth on deforested land and steep terrains.

by Euglossini, while a few appear to be pollinated by
hummingbirds.

Belize.

62. Arpophyllum La Llave & Lex.
Epiphytic, lithophytic or terrestrial herbs. Rhizome
stout, creeping. Stems unifoliate, more or less
enclosed in sheaths. Leaves leathery or fleshy. In-
florescences terminal, from a large sheath. Flowers

all native to the American tropics. One is known from
Belize.

arching, linear, leathery, up to 65 cm long and 3 cm
wide. Inflorescence densely flowered, up to 30 cm
long, with the cylindrical raceme up to 2.5 cm in
diameter; sheath flattened, up to 14 cm long;
peduncle up to 16 cm long. Flowers showy, purple-
pink; pedicellate ovaries up to 7 mm long. Sepals up
to 6 mm long and 3 mm wide; lateral sepals concave
at the base. Petals with somewhat undulate margins,
up to 5.5 mm long and 1.8 mm wide. Lip curved,
concave, broadly rounded and minutely toothed at
the apex, clasping the column in the front of the
pouch-like base, up to 6.5 mm long and 4 mm wide.
Column arcuate, up to 4 mm long. (Fig. 74; Photo.
126).

ca), Mexico to Costa Rica, Colombia and Venezuela.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Cayo and Toledo Dis-
tricts. Locally common.
HABITAT. On rocks, logs and trees in the moist to
wet broad-leaved forest between 600 and 750 m.
FLOWERING SEASON. February to April. Flowers
last about ten days.
EtymoLogY. From the Latin giganteus (unusually
large of tall) in reference to the plant size.

spicatum but, according to Garay (1974), the latter
occurs only in Mexico and differs in its charact-
istically shaped, folded and fleshy leaves. Correll
(1965) and Siegerist (1984) reported A. spicatum
from Belize on the basis of a specimen at MO which
could not be found (Catling & Catling 1988).

Plant terrestrial, lithophytic or epiphytic, erect
spreading, up to 55 cm tall. Pseudobulbs clustered,
ovoid, somewhat flattened, pale green, finely
wrinkled, 3- to 5-leaved, up to 6.5 cm long and 4.5
cm wide, enclosed in rigid sheaths when young.
Leaves linear-elliptic, acuminate, somewhat leathery,
up to 55 cm long and 3.5 cm wide; sheaths up to 17
cm long, toothed at the apex after the leaves fall.
Inflorescence erect, 3- to 5-flowered, up to 16 cm tall;
peduncle short; sheaths overlapping, more or less
rigid, glossy; floral bracts large, similar to the
sheaths. Flowers showy, fragrant; pedicellate ovaries
up to 3.3 cm long. Sepals erect below, spreading
above, white with rose-pink tips, up to 1 cm wide;
dorsal sepal up to 3.3 cm long; lateral sepals oblique,
up to 5 cm long to the base of the mentum. Petals
white, up to 3.1 cm long and 1 cm wide. Lip white,
suffused with yellow on the mid-lobe and below,
narrow and pouch-like at the base, abruptly bent
above the basal portion, up to 4.5 cm long and 1.5 cm
wide across the lateral lobes when spread; mid-lobe
triangular, decurved, thickened in the centre. Column
white, with a yellow foot about 2 cm long. (Fig. 75;
Photo. 127).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Mexico to Honduras.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Cayo and Toledo Dis-
tricts. Uncommon.
HABITAT. Terrestrial or on rocks or trees in moist
to wet broad-leaved forest between 600 and 750 m.
FLOWERING SEASON. November to January.
Flowers last about five days.
ETymoLoGY. From the Latin bellus (somewhat
beautiful).
64 Brassavola
SUBTRIBE LAELIINAE BENTH.
Epiphytic herbs, sometimes growing on rocks. Rhi-
zome commonly short. Stems slender or thickened
and pseudobulbous, unifolate, enclosed in sheaths
when young. Leaves fleshy. Inflorescences com-
monly terminal, rarely lateral, 1- to several-flowered.
Flowers large and showy. Sepals and petals similar.
Lip simple or three-lobed, tubular at base, more or
less enclosing the column, with or without a basal
callus. Column erect, short, mostly 2-winged; anther
operculate; pollinia 8.
A genus of about 15 species, all native to the
American tropics. Four are known from Belize.
The predominantly white or pale greenish flowers
are usually pollinated by moths.
Several species are widely cultivated and some
have been extensively used in the production of horti-
cultural hybrids. The majority of crosses have in-
volved species of Cattleya and Laelia, giving rise to
the hybrid genera x Brassocattleya, x Brassolaelia
and x Brassolaeliocattleya.
H.G. Jones (1975) revised the sectional limits of
Brassavola. Section Grandiflora, in which the leaves
are flat and broad, corresponds to Rhyncolaelia
Schltr. and was excluded by Schlechter (1919) from
his revision and by us here.
EtymoLogY. Named after the Venetian nobleman
and botanist Antonio Musa Brassavola (1500-1555).

A genus of about 30 species, all in the American
tropics and most numerous in Brazil. One is known
from Belize.

vated of all orchid genera. A vast array of horticul-

GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Belize, Guatemala(?)
and Honduras.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Belize and Cayo (in-
cluding the Mountain Pine Ridge Reserve) Districts.
Locally common.
HABITAT. On granite outcrops, cliffs, ravine sides
and limestone rocks between 100 and 1000 m.
Rarely found on trees in pine/oak forest.
FLOWERING SEASON. July to October. Flowers last
about two weeks.
EtymoLogY. Named after J.C. Bowring (1821-
1893) of Windsor, England, who was an enthusiastic
amateur grower of orchids.
NoTES. Almost confined to the Mountain Pine
Ridge Reserve where it is often found in association
with Encyclia belizensis subsp. belizensis. Halcrow
& Halcrow (1967) reported a white-flowered form
but we have never seen it. C. bowringiana has been
considered by some authors to be no more than a
geographic variant of the more widespread C. skin-
neri Batem. It differs from C. skinneri principally in
having bulbous stem bases and in tending to grow
larger in favourable situations such as along the Rio
On, the type locality. The flowering season is also
atypical of C. skinneri which is normally spring-
fowering.
Several authors have reported both C. bowringiana
and C. skinneri from Belize but we have been quite
unable to find the latter in the field. Plants on exposed
rocks are generally much smaller than those in shel-
tered ravines and a rare individual may flower outside
the normal season but every one of the many we have
examined has proved to have the bulbous stem bases
typical of C. bowringiana.
Epiphytic herbs. Pseudobulbs clustered, elongate,
several-jointed, bearing 2- several terminal leaves,
more or less enclosed in sheaths when young. Leaves
leathery. Inflorescences terminal, few- to many-
flowered; peduncle elongate. Flowers in a raceme
and rather showy. Sepals and petals similar, spread-
ing. Lip 3-lobed, provided with a pair of hollow
horn-like calli. Column short, winged; anther ter-
minal; pollinia 4, waxy.
There are only two species, both confined to the
American tropics. One is known from Belize.

arthron (joint) referring to the several-jointed pseu-
dobulbs.

Plant epiphytic, erect, a cluster of cane-like stems, up
to 40 cm tall. Stem tapering above and below. Leaves
distichous, leathery, linear-oblong, unevenly notched
at the tip, up to 15 cm long and 1.3 cm wide. Inflores-
cence a few-flowered raceme at the top of each stem
with, normally, only one flower developing at a time.

Plant epiphytic, more or less erect, up to 22 cm tall.
Pseudobulbs clustered, ovoid to subcircular, strongly
flattened, 2- or 3-leaved, up to 3 cm long and wide,
subtended by sheaths when young. Leaves recurved,
narrowly elliptic to oblanceolate, glossy, up to 13 cm
long and 1.7 cm wide. Inflorescence from a promi-
nent sheath, few-flowered, up to 18 cm long; sheath
flattened, up to 6 cm long; peduncle up to 8 cm long.
Flowers in a raceme; pedicellate ovaries slender,
about 1.5 cm long, often developing into conspi-
cuously 3-winged capsules before the flowers fade.
Sepals and petals greenish-yellow with brown
blotches, with more or less recurved margins, up to
1.2 cm long and 4.5 mm wide. Lip joined to the lower
third of the column, obscurely 3-lobed, pale
greenish-yellow, up to 9 mm long and 7 mm wide
when spread; lateral lobes deflexed, triangular; mid-
lobe fleshy-thickened; callus oblanceolate, white, 3-
toothed at the apex, grooved below the middle. Col-
umn arcuate, greenish, tipped with pale yellow,
blotched with purple at the base, up to 5.5 mm long.
(Fig. 83L; Photo. 139).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Southern Florida, Cuba,
the West Indies, Mexico and Belize.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Orange Walk,
and Cayo Districts. Uncommon.
HABITAT. On trees and shrubs in rather dry forest
and shrub below 100 m.
FLOWERING SEASON. August to October. Flowers
last about three weeks.
ETyMoLoGY. Named after William Beattie Booth
(1804-1879) an English botanist from whose descrip-
tion Lindley based his report.
NoTE. Commonly known as the 'Dollar' orchid on
account of the coin- shaped pseudobulbs.

NOTES. The plants we found resembled E. belizen-
sis with flowers similar to those of E asperula.

ary and tooth-like. Of all the material we have seen,
they appear nearest to the type of E. chloroleuca and
we believe they can be referred to that species,
despite the fact that it is otherwise only known from
northeastern South America.

68 Encyclia
masses, stout and creeping, 0.6 cm in diameter, from

cm long and 0.4 mm wide, recurved with a central
vein; petals slightly shorter, spathulate. Lip simple,
adnate to the lower half of the column, concave,
creamy-white with 9 short purplish veins; two short
lateral lobes point upwards and forewards; central
lobe curving upwards, acuminate, with two falcate
whitish calli; up to 18.5 mm long. Column with
prominent downward pointing wings, greenish-white
with a bright yellow apex, up to 5.5 mm long. (Fig.
82H; Photo. 149).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Mexico to Honduras,
and Costa Rica.

fibre) in reference to the purple veins on the lip.

and 3 mm wide. Petals porrect, oblanceolate, green
with more or less undulate margins, up to 11 mm long
and 4 mm wide. Lip basally adnate to the column,
3-lobed, up to 10 mm long; lateral lobes oblong,
clasping the column, white above, purple below, up to
5.5 x 2.3 mm; mid-lobe suborbicular with lateral
margins upcurved, white marked with purple on
about 12 raised veins in the centre, undulate margins,
up to 5 mm long and 6 mm wide when spread; callus
of four ridges. Column slightly bowed, winged, green
edged with white, up to 4.5 mm long; wings subqua-
drate, incurved. (Fig. 81M; Photo. 151).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Belize.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Cayo (Mountain Pine
Ridge Reserve) and Toledo Districts. Rare.
HABITAT. In wet broadleaved forest between 700
and 950 m.
FLOWERING SEASON. August to November.
EtymoLogY. From the Latin porrectus (streched
outwards) in reference to the petal attitude.
NOTES. E porrecta is closely related to E. cera-
tistes (Lindl.) Schltr. & E chloroleuca (Hook.)
Neum. but differsin having exceptionallysmall
flowers with porrect petals. It is further distinguished
from E. ceratistes by having well developed subqua-
drate wings on a short column and from E. chloroleu-
ca by the verrucose inflorescence branches and ova-
ries.
22. Encyclia pygmaea (Hook.) Dressler in Brittonia
13: 264 (1961). Type: Brazil, A. Harrison s.n. (holo.
K!).
Epidendrum pygmaeum Hook. in Bot. Mag. 60: t.
3233 (1833).
E. caespitosum Poepp. & Endl., Nov. Gen. Sp. 2: 1,
t.101(1838).
Hormidium pygmaeum (Hook.) Benth. & Hook. in
Biol. Centr.-Am. Bot. 3: 218 (1883).
H. tripterum (Brongn.) Cogn. in Mart., Fl. Bras. 3,
pt.S : 29 (1898).
Microstylis humilis Cogn. in Mart., Fl. Bras. 3(6):
550, t.114 (1906).
Plant epiphytic, low growing, creeping, rhizomatous.
Rhizome branching. Pseudobulbs 3-5 cm apart on the
rhizome, ovoid, up to 5 cm long and 8 mm in diame-
68 Encyclia
ter, normally two apical leaves. Leaves narrowly
ovate, up to 5.5 cm long and 1.5 cm wide. Inflores-
cence terminal, 1-flowered. Flowers up to 1.2 cm in
diameter, fragrant. Sepals and petals similar, cream to
pale green, lanceolate, up to 6 mm long and 3 mm
wide. Lip 3-lobed, adnate to the base of the column,
free part clawed, white with 1-3 purple streaks, up to
4.5 mm long. Column short, up to 3 mm long. (Fig.
84; Photo. 152).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Florida, the West Indies,
Mexico to Peru, Bolivia and Brazil.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Cayo (including Moun-
tain Pine Ridge Reserve) and Toledo Districts. Fairly
common.
HABITAT. On trees in dense, often moist forest.
FLOWERING SEASON. July to February.
ETYmoLoGY. From the Latin pygmeus (dwarf) in
reference to the dwarf growth habit.
NOTE. When not in flower E. Pygmaea may be
confused with E polybulbon which, however, is a
smaller plant and occurs in dryer environments.
23. Encyclia radiata (Lindl.) Dressler in Brittonia
4: 214 (1856). Type: Mexico, cult. Loddiges (holo.
К.).
Epidendrum radiatum Lindl. in Bot. Reg. 27: Misc.
58 (1841).
Plant epiphytic, low growing, creeping. Rhizome
bearing erect pseudobulbs 2.5 cm apart. Pseudobulbs
ellipsoid, ribbed and flattened, 2- to 3-leaves, up to 16
cm long and 4 cm wide. Leaves lanceolate-elliptic,
acute, up to 30 cm long and 2.8 cm wide. Inflores-
cence apically from the pseudobulb, 2- to 8-flowers
together in a cluster, up to 20 cm long. Flowers 3 cm
in diameter, strongly fragrant, non-resupinate;
flowers yellow with age. Sepals and petals subsimi-
lar, pale green, up to 20 mm long; sepals up to 7 mm
wide; petals up to 1 mm wide. Lip triangular-
reniform, concave, whitish to pale yellow and veined
with purple, up to 13 mm long and 20 mm wide;
callus quadrate, smooth. Column stout with a fan-
shaped ligule, up to 10 mm long. (Fig. 82J; Photo.
153).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Mexico to Costa Rica,
and Venezuela.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Cayo (including the
Mountain Pine Ridge Reserve) and Stann Creek Dis-
tricts. Uncommon.
HABITAT. Usually on oaks in broken forest.
FLOWERING SEASON. Intermittent throughout the
year. Flowers last several weeks.
EtymoLogY. From the Latin radiatus (radiating
outwards).

dendrum and the Greek anthos (flower), alluding to
the Epidendrum-like flowers and the fact that the
species were once included within that genus.
Epidanthus paranthicus (Rchb. f.) LO.Williams in
Bot. Mus. Leafl. Harvard. Univ. 8: 148 (1940). Type:
Guatemala, Warszewicz s.n. (holo. W!).
Epidendrum paranthicum Rchb. f. in Bot. Zeit. 10:
Plant creeping to hanging, often forming dense
masses. Rhizome slender, branching, enclosed in
sheaths, up to 60 cm long. Stem about 2.5 cm apart,
slightly flattened, up to 9-leaved, up to 10 cm long.
Leaves terete, somewhat recurved, up to 2.5 cm long
and 1.5 mm wide. Inflorescence loosely 5- to 7-
flowered, up to 4 cm long; peduncle slender. Flowers
greenish-yellow, somewhat fleshy; pedicellate ova-
ries up to 2.5 cm long. Sepals keeled, about 3 mm
long and 1.5 mm wide; dorsal sepal recurved; lateral
sepals spreading. Petals recurved, up to 3 mm long
and 1 mm wide. Lip 3-lobed, up to 3 mm long and 3
mm wide; lateral lobes erect, clasping the column,
rounded; mid-lobe very slender, antenna-like; disc
with a fleshy callus on the central portion. Column
about 1 mm long, fleshy. (Fig. 85; Photo. 154, 155).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Mexico to Panama.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Cayo District (in-
cluding the Mountain Pine Ridge Reserve). Rare.
HABITAT. On trees in rather wet broad-leaved
forest at about 900 m.
FLOWERING SEASON. July and August. Flowers
last two to three weeks.
EtymologY. Perhaps from the Greek para (near,
beside) and anthos (flower).
Epiphytic, terrestrial or lithophytic plants, very small
to large, erect or creeping. Stems usually not
pseudobulbous, caulescent, rarely pseudobulbous,
branched, 1- to many-leaved. Leaves linear to ovate,
terete to flattened. Inflorescences usually terminal,
racemose, subumbellate to paniculate. Flowers small
to large and showy. Sepals and petals spreading. Lip
adnate to the column-apex, lamina entire to 3-lobed,
smooth to callose. Column short to elongate, win-
gless or winged; pollinia 4, waxy, usually lacking a
stipe.
One of the largest genera with several hundred

Americas from N. Carolina to Argentina. Twenty two
are known from Belize.
Epidendrum plants are generally pollinated by
moths and butterflies, although some groups, espe-
cially those with orange, red or purple flowers, parti-
cularly the E. ibaguense complex, are pollinated by
hummingbirds.

dron (tree) referring tothe epiphytic habit of most
species.

1. Epidendrum acuñae Dressler in Am. Orch. Soc.
Bull. 28: 358 (1959). Type: Cuba, C. Wright 3333
(holo. MO; iso. AMES, G, K, P, W).
Spathiger roigii Acuña in Estac. Exper. Agron. Bot.
Tec. 60:93 (1939) nom. illeg.
Plant epiphytic, with one to several segmented stems,
somewhat- to much-branched, up to 2-3 m long and
4-5 mm wide, with persistent brown sheaths. Leaves
produced distichously, 2.5-3 cm apart, lower leaves
deciduous with age, leathery, strap-shaped, slightly
notched at the apex, up to 15 cm long and 1.5 cm
wide; the leaves on the main stems are longer than
leaves on flowering branches. Inflorescence terminal,
flowers born singly on short side branches. Flowers
fragrant during the day, up to 1.3 cm long and 1.8 cm
wide; pedicellate ovary covered with overlapping
bracts which are finely purple-spotted. Sepals green-
ish with margins rolled back, up to 1.5 cm long.
Petals paler green, suffused with purple at base, up to
1.5 cm long. Lip pale green, suffused with purple at
base, fleshy, up to 1.2 cm long and 6 mm wide; callus
slender, runnung down centre of lip. Column winged,
toothed at apex, up to 5 mm long and 4 mm wide.
(Fig. 86K; Photo. 156).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Florida, Cuba, Mexico,
Belize, Guatemala, Costa Rica and Panama.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Cayo District. Rare.
HABITAT. On trees in moist forest.
FLOWERING SEASON. May and June. Flowers last
about two weeks.
EtymoLoGY. Named after Galé Acuña who first
named the species but gave it an invalid name.

ternate, white, showy, fragrant, about 10 cm across,

E. alexandri Schltr., Anex. Mem. Inst. Butantan 1(4):
E. rantierium Lindl. ex Sanchez., Orq. Mex. 47
Plant epiphytic or terrestrial, erect, growing in
clumps, up to 1.3 m tall. Stem numerous, reed-like.
Leaves distichous, oblong-elliptic, erect, leathery, up
to 23 cm long and 4 cm wide; leaf-sheath enveloping
the stem, up to 6 cm long; leaves deciduous, falling
from the lower part of the stem first leaving the
leaf-sheaths. Inflorescence terminal, racemose, pen-
dulous, up to 30 cm long; peduncle covered with
large papery spathe-like bracts. Flowers several,
opening together, slightly fragrant, up to 3 cm in
diameter. Sepals and petals similar, green with purple
spots; sepals up to 2.8 cm long and 8 mm wide; petals
up to 2.6 cm long and 5 mm wide. Lip adnate to the
column-apex, irregularly 3-lobed, white base with
purple spots and greenish towards the margins, up to
1.5 cm long; disc with a two lobed callus and a central
ridge. Column club-shaped, white, up to 1.5 cm long.
(Photo. 158).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Mexico to Honduras,
and northern South America.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Cayo and Toledo Dis-
tricts. Uncommon.
HABITAT. Terrestrial or on trees and rotten logs in
moist forest.
FLOWERING SEASON. May and June, September
and October. Flowers last two to three weeks.
ETymoLoGY. From the Latin cristatus (crested,
tassel-like at the tips) in reference to the appearance
of the side lobes of the lip.
NoTE. Catling & Catling (1988) excluded E
cristatum on the basis of a revision by E. Hágsater of
a Gentle specimen reported by Correll (1965) and
used the name E. raniferum Lindl. We consider them
as synonymous and therefore use the earlier name.

5. Epidendrum cystosum Ames in Bot. Mus. Leafl.
Harvard Univ. 2: 106 (1934). Type: Honduras, Yoro,
J. B. Edwards 675 (holo. AMES).
Plant epiphytic, up to 13 cm tall. Roots fibrous,
smooth. Stem caespitose, erect, up to 5.5 cm long,
with 6 leaves. Leaves ascending, linear-lanceolate, up
to 5.5 cm long and 6 mm wide. Inflorescence few-
flowered, usually 1 flower open at any time; rachis of
raceme up to 7 mm long; bracts infundibuliform, up
to 2.5 mm long. Flowers with sepals and petals light
lavender and lip greenish-yellow with lavender mar-
gin. Lateral sepals lanceolate, up to 9 mm long and 3
mm wide; dorsal sepal similar. Petals linear, up to 8.5
mm long. Lip adnate to column, up to 8 mm long; free
portion concave, up to 5 mm long and 5 mm wide,
fleshy, rigid; callus elongate. Column up to 3.5 mm
long.
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Belize and Honduras.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Toledo District. Rare.
HABITAT. On trees in damp forest.
FLOWERING SEASON. April.
EtymologY. From the Greek cysto (hollow,
pouched) in reference to the concave lip.

and fleshy, elliptic-lanceolate, up to 10 cm long and 3
cm wide. Inflorescence terminal, subumbellate, 1- to
18-flowered, with all the flowers opening together.
Flowers strongly fragrant, pale green or whitish, up
to 2.8 cm in diameter; bracts hyaline; pedicellate
ovaries up to 4 cm long. Sepals and petals similar,
slender, up to 3.2 cm long and 8 mm wide. Lip adnate
to the column-apex; lamina simple to 3-lobed, up to
1.8 cm long and 3.4 cm wide, transversely kidney-
shaped; disc with two small calli at base. Column
dilated above, up to 10 mm long. (Fig. 92J; Photo.

Mexico to northern South America.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Cayo (including the
Mountain Pine Ridge Reserve) and Toledo Districts.
Uncommon.

7. Epidendrum diffusum Sw., Prod. Veg. Ind. Occ.:
121 (1788). Type: Jamaica, Swartz (holo. S).
Seraphyta diffusa (Sw.) Pfitzer ex Fawc. & Rendle,
Plant epiphytic or terrestrial, erect-spreading. Stem
reed-like, reddish-purple, flattened, lower part cov-
ered with papery leaf-sheaths. Leaves distichous, up
to 16 on the upper part of the stem, oblong-elliptic,
leathery, dark green, strongly tinged with purple on
the edges and beneath, up to 7 cm long and 2.5 cm
wide. Inflorescence terminal, diffuse, branched,
many-flowered, up to 27 cm long. Flowers small, up
to 1 cm in diameter, reddish-brown; pedicellate ova-
ries up to 5 mm long. Sepals lanceolate, acute, up to 9
mm long and 2.3 mm wide. Petals spreading, fili-
form, reflexed, up to 8 mm long and less than 1 mm
wide. Lip adnate with the column,heart-shaped,
pointed at the apex, up to 7 mm long and 5 mm wide;
disc with a 3-pronged callus. Column greenish, up to
4 mm long. (Fig. 92K; Photo. 160).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Cuba, the West Indies,
Mexico to Colombia, Surinam and Brazil.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Cayo District (includ-
ing the Mountain Pine Ridge Reserve). Uncommon.
HABITAT. In open pine/oak forest.
FLOWERING SEASON. August and September.
Flowers last several weeks.
ETYmoLoGY. From the Latin diffusus (loosely
spreading) in reference to the rather diffuse pani-
culate inflorescence.
8. Epidendrum hawkesii A. H. Heller in Phytologia
14:2 (1966). Type: Nicaragua, Zelaya, A. H. Heller &
A. D. Hawkes 8344 (holo. F).
Plant epiphytic, rarely terrestrial. Stem crowded,
simple, rigidly erect, with profuse basal white
branching roots, up to 1 m tall, concealed at base by
sheaths flushed dark purple. Leaves oblong-elliptic,
concave,retuse apex,leathery, mottled or spotted
with dull purple, up to 11 cm long and 4.5 cm wide.
Inflorescence compact, densely many-flowered, 20-

to 60-flowered, racemose; peduncle up to 50 cm
long; floral bracts triangular-ovate, up to 4 mm long.
Flowers very showy, up to 3 cm long and 2.5 cm
wide, spreading, carmine with dark yellow calli on
the lip, column-apex yellow; anther cap apple-green;
pedicellate ovary erect, up to 5 cm long. Sepals and
petals acute, nervose; dorsal sepal oblanceolate, up to
1.5 cm long and 4.5 mm wide; lateral sepal oblique,
up to 1.6 cm long and 4 mm wide; petals 7-nerved,
obovate, acute, up to 1.5 cm long and 5.5 mm wide.
Lip adnate to the column, 3-lobed, up to 8 mm long
and 1.2 cm wide, margins serrated; mid-lobe sepa-
rated from laterals by a 3 mm isthmus; disc with 2
prominent flap-like calli. Column straight, clavate, up
to 1 cm long. (Fig. 86; Photo. 161).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Central America.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Stann Creek District.
Rare.
HABITAT. On trees in citrus plantations, rarely
terrestrial.
FLOWERING SEASON. February to July. Flowers
last one to two weeks.
EtymoLogy. Named after Alex Hawkes, who was
the junior author of the original description.
NoTES. E. ibaguense Kunth, has been reported
from Belize by Correll (1965) but the supporting
specimens cannot be found. It is thought that these
reports were a misidentification of E. hawkesii (Cat-
ling & Catling, 1988). Although these plants are
similar E. hawkesii differs from E ibaguense in hav-
ing roots that are basal only, rather larger leaves of a
divergent shape, flowers of a vivid carmine-lake with
dark yellow calli and column apex, a lip that is deeply
3-lobed and basally truncate, a disc with 2 prominent
flap-like calli at the base and a prominent erect sig-
moid keel extending from the base to the apex of the
lip.

HABITAT. In open pine/oak forest.
FLOWERING SEASON. August and September.
Flowers last several weeks.
ETYmoLoGY. From the Latin diffusus (loosely
spreading) in reference to the rather diffuse pani-
culate inflorescence.
8. Epidendrum hawkesii A. H. Heller in Phytologia
14:2 (1966). Type: Nicaragua, Zelaya, A. H. Heller &
A. D. Hawkes 8344 (holo. F).
Plant epiphytic, rarely terrestrial. Stem crowded,
simple, rigidly erect, with profuse basal white
branching roots, up to 1 m tall, concealed at base by
sheaths flushed dark purple. Leaves oblong-elliptic,
concave,retuse apex,leathery, mottled or spotted
with dull purple, up to 11 cm long and 4.5 cm wide.
Inflorescence compact, densely many-flowered, 20-
70 Epidendrum
to 60-flowered, racemose; peduncle up to 50 cm
long; floral bracts triangular-ovate, up to 4 mm long.
Flowers very showy, up to 3 cm long and 2.5 cm
wide, spreading, carmine with dark yellow calli on
the lip, column-apex yellow; anther cap apple-green;
pedicellate ovary erect, up to 5 cm long. Sepals and
petals acute, nervose; dorsal sepal oblanceolate, up to
1.5 cm long and 4.5 mm wide; lateral sepal oblique,
up to 1.6 cm long and 4 mm wide; petals 7-nerved,
obovate, acute, up to 1.5 cm long and 5.5 mm wide.
Lip adnate to the column, 3-lobed, up to 8 mm long
and 1.2 cm wide, margins serrated; mid-lobe sepa-
rated from laterals by a 3 mm isthmus; disc with 2
prominent flap-like calli. Column straight, clavate, up
to 1 cm long. (Fig. 86; Photo. 161).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Central America.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Stann Creek District.
Rare.
HABITAT. On trees in citrus plantations, rarely
terrestrial.
FLOWERING SEASON. February to July. Flowers
last one to two weeks.
EtymoLogy. Named after Alex Hawkes, who was
the junior author of the original description.
NoTES. E. ibaguense Kunth, has been reported
from Belize by Correll (1965) but the supporting
specimens cannot be found. It is thought that these
reports were a misidentification of E. hawkesii (Cat-
ling & Catling, 1988). Although these plants are
similar E. hawkesii differs from E ibaguense in hav-
ing roots that are basal only, rather larger leaves of a
divergent shape, flowers of a vivid carmine-lake with
dark yellow calli and column apex, a lip that is deeply
3-lobed and basally truncate, a disc with 2 prominent
flap-like calli at the base and a prominent erect sig-
moid keel extending from the base to the apex of the
lip.

Orch. PL.: 106 (1831). Type: Guyana, Parkin s.n.
