10. Epidendrum isomerum Schltr. in Fedde, Re-
pert. Nov. Sp. 2: 132 (1906). Type: Guatemala, H. von
Türckheim 167 (holo. Bt; lecto. US).
Epidendrum guayaense Schltr. in Fedde, Repert.
Spec. Nov. Beih. 8: 73 (1921).
Plant epiphytic, in dense clumps. Stem wiry, pendu-
lous, often branched, up to 115 cm long; aerial roots
often produced along the stem. Leaves distichous, 1
cm apart, deciduous in lower parts with age, long-
linear, pointed, up to 10 cm long and 7 mm wide.
Inflorescence terminal with a single flower. Flower
fragrant, greenish, yellowing with age, up to 2 cm in
diameter, sessile; pedicellate ovary stout, concealed
by subtending bracts. Sepals and petals similar,
linear-lanceolate; sepals up to 1.3 cm long and 2 mm
wide; petals up to 1.3 cm long and 1.5 mm wide. Lip
adnate to the column, triangular-lanceolate, chan-
nelled, up to 1.2 cm long with a free terminal portion
of up to 0.9 cm long; callus linear, sulcate. Column
straight, up to 5 mm long, clinandrium bilobed, sur-
70 Epidendrum
passing the column. (Fig. 92M; Photo. 164).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Mexico to Panama.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Cayo, Stann Creek and
Toledo Districts. Uncommon.
HABITAT. On trees in moist forest and citrus plan-
tations.
FLOWERING SEASON. August to October. Flowers
last seven to ten days.
EtymoLoGY. From the Greek iso (equal) and
meros (parts) presumably in reference to the similar-
ity between the sepals and petals.
11. Epidendrum macroclinium E. Hágsater in Or-
quídea (México) 10(2): 319 (1987). Type: Mexico,
Chiapas, Thurston T-1952 in Hágsater 5484 (holo.
AMO).
Plant epiphytic, small, low growing, creeping habit,
up to 30 cm tall. Stem somewhat flattened, complete-
ly enclosed in leaf-sheaths, up to 13 cm long and 0.2
cm in diameter. Leaves several, alternate along the
length of the stem, lanceolate, thickened, fleshy, up to
3.5 cm long and 0.9 cm wide. Inflorescence terminal,
branched, up to 17.5 cm long; peduncle segmented,
very slender, enclosed in dry papery sheaths. Flowers
produced in sequence, only one open at a time, not
scented, up to 1 cm in diameter; pedicellate ovary
pink, with a sack-like vesicle about 0.2 cm in diame-
ter just behind the lip. Sepals oblong, semi-
transparent pink, up to 0.6 cm long and 0.3 cm wide.
Petals slender, up to 0.6 cm long and 0.1 cm wide. Lip
adnate to the column, obreniform, base cuniform,
lamina tubular, whitish, up to 0.6 cm long; lateral
lobes semicircular; callus near base of each lobe.
Column up to 5 mm long; clinandrium prominent.
(Fig. 86L; Photo. 165).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Mexico to Panama.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Cayo and Toledo Dis-
tricts. Very rare.
HABITAT. On trees in moist forest.
FLOWERING SEASON. December to March.
Flowers last one to two weeks.
ETYMoLoGY. From the Greek macro (large) and
cline (a bed or couch) in reference to the large clinan-
drium.
NoTES. E physodes Rchb. f. has been reported
from Belize but Hágsater (1987) has examined these
specimens and found them to be E macroclinium. E.
physodes appears to be restricted to Costa Rica.

Am.: 82 (1866). Type: Guatemala, Las Nubes, H.
Wendland (holo. W, not located).

lines.text: Epidendrum johannis Schltr. in Fedde, Repert. Sp.
Plant epiphytic, creeping, branched rhizomes which
give rise to several erect stems. Stems flattened, up to
21 cm long, almost totally covered with leaf-sheaths
which are green at first, becoming brown and papery
after the leaf-blades have fallen. Leaves distichous,
3-4 cm apart, thickened, shiny, up to 15.5 cm long and
2.5 cm wide. Inflorescence terminal, up to 15 cm
long, with up to 11 distichous flowers; ovaries and
lower parts of flower concealed by fleshy green
floral-bracts. Flowers fleshy, entirely greenish, not
fragrant, sessile; pedicellate ovary up to 8 mm long.
Dorsal sepal up to 1.2 cm long and 4 mm wide,
opening upwards. Lateral sepals up to 1.2 cm long
and 4 mm wide, keeled at the apex, clasping the petals
against the lip. Petals up to 1.1 cm long and 1 mm
wide. Lip adnate to the column, slightly contracted in
the middle of each side, up to 8 mm long and 7 mm
wide; disc bicallose at base. Column bilobed at the
apex, up to 6 mm long. (Photo. 166).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Mexico, Belize, Guate-
mala and Costa Rica.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Toledo District. Un-
common.
HABITAT. On trees in dense wet forest.
FLOWERING SEASON. September and October.
Flowers last individually two to three weeks.
EtymoLoGY. From the Latin nitens (shiny, glossy)
in reference to the shiny appearance of the flowers.
NOTE. E. nitens is probably the plant listed by
Caroline Whitfoord as E. coriifolium (1791, K!).

Plant epiphytic, a cluster of reed-like stems up to 60

wide; stem covered with leaf-sheaths, initially green,
becoming brown and papery with age. Leaves dis-

from old inflorescences even when the stems are

Toledo Districts. Common.
HABITAT. On trees and shrubs in moist forest, and
citrus plantations.
FLOWERING SEASON. June to October, and Febru-
ary.
EtymologY. From the Latin nocturnus (night-
flowering).
NOTE. This plant is commonly known as the
